In the last layers, Lithuanian sends 55-72% of expert selections to eight experts, against 19-39% for English.
AI.conclusion: Calibration transfer is asymmetric, and the concentration of Lithuanian routing on a few experts helps explain why English calibration erodes Lithuanian performance.

title: Continued Training of Continuous Language Flows with Token Identity Squared Supervision
summary: Diffusion and flow models have recently been extended to language modeling, generating text through continuous denoising in token embedding spaces. Pretrained models provide token representations and contextual prediction capabilities, but improving generation with limited additional training requires an appropriate connection between supervision and continuous generation. Continuous MSE evaluates a predicted vector obtained by weighting token embeddings with predicted probabilities; different probability distributions can yield the same vector and are therefore indistinguishable under this objective. We propose Token Identity Brier Flow (TIBF), which applies squared supervision directly to token identities when continuing pretrained language flows. TIBF combines network scores with token-matching scores under a Gaussian observation model, supervises token probabilities using the Brier loss, and uses probability-weighted embeddings for continuous generation. With fixed token embeddings, we show that the squared error between predicted token probabilities and the true posterior bounds the squared errors of continuous denoising predictions and flow velocities. A risk decomposition separates uncertainty inherent in the observation from posterior fitting error, motivating continued training that preserves pretrained embeddings and focuses on probability prediction. We also establish convergence to token embeddings under ideal predictions and sufficient conditions for local convergence with prediction error. From common pretrained initializations and under matched continuation budgets, frozen-embedding TIBF achieves this http URL values of 33.96 on OWT and 81.17 on LM1B, outperforming continuous-MSE and CE continuation controls. It attains the lowest this http URL at every tested sampling budget on both datasets, together with the lowest repetition rate on LM1B.

AI.tldr: TIBF continues pretrained continuous language flows by applying the Brier loss directly to token identity probabilities, outperforming continuous-MSE and cross-entropy continuation controls.
AI.motivation: Continuous MSE evaluates a vector formed by weighting token embeddings with predicted probabilities, so different probability distributions can yield the same vector and are indistinguishable under that objective.
AI.method: TIBF combines network scores with token-matching scores under a Gaussian observation model, supervises token probabilities with the Brier loss, and generates through probability-weighted embeddings, keeping pretrained token embeddings frozen.
AI.result: Under matched continuation budgets, frozen-embedding TIBF reaches values of 33.96 on OWT and 81.17 on LM1B, outperforming the controls, and attains the lowest value at every tested sampling budget on both datasets, with the lowest repetition rate on LM1B (the metric name is garbled in the abstract).
AI.conclusion: Squared supervision on token identities, backed by a risk decomposition and convergence results, offers a principled way to continue training pretrained language flows by focusing on probability prediction.

title: O$^2$PD: Overlap-Gated On-Policy Distillation on Reliable Prefix
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) supplies dense token-level supervision by aligning a student to the teacher's next-token distribution on its own generated rollouts. Existing works mostly implement top-$k$ OPD, applying reverse Kullback-Leibler ($\RKL$) divergence between the teacher's and the student's renormalized distributions over teacher top-$k$ support. However, the teacher scores student-generated rollouts that are inherently off-policy for itself, leaving the reliability of its next-token guidance unclear. Restricting the divergence to the teacher top-$k$ support also discards the remaining mass outside that support. These gaps leave two questions implicit: 1) which tokens to align, and 2) how to align those tokens. To answer these questions, we propose Overlap-gated On-Policy Distillation (O$^{2}$PD). As for 1), we quantitatively analyze the reliability of teacher supervision and find that alignment on the student's trajectory prefix is more reliable than alignment on the full context. Therefore, our O$^{2}$PD is applied only to the 20\% prefix tokens of each student rollout. As for 2), we theoretically characterize two problems of top-$k$ OPD: the \emph{Teacher-support Uncovering} and the \emph{Dominant-Mode Mismatch}. Based on these analyses, we propose two support strategies: the \emph{Reset Support} strategy attaches a reset atom to every token, pooling mass outside the teacher top-$k$, and the \emph{Support Convergence} strategy converges the support to the already aligned intersection. Our O$^{2}$PD employs the designed overlap-gated $\alpha$-divergence to interpolate between mode-covering and mode-seeking for per-token alignment, where the overlap is used as a gate to switch the support and adaptively modulate $\alpha$.

AI.tldr: O2PD applies overlap-gated on-policy distillation to the first 20% prefix tokens of student rollouts, with support strategies that address the limits of top-k distillation.
AI.motivation: Top-k on-policy distillation applies reverse KL to off-policy student rollouts scored by the teacher, and restricting the divergence to the teacher's top-k support discards the mass outside it, leaving which tokens to align and how to align them unresolved.
AI.method: Alignment is restricted to the 20% prefix tokens of each student rollout; Reset Support pools mass outside the teacher top-k with a reset atom, Support Convergence converges support to the aligned intersection, and an overlap-gated alpha-divergence interpolates between mode-covering and mode-seeking alignment.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: Alignment on the prefix is more reliable than alignment on the full context, and the two support strategies address the Teacher-support Uncovering and Dominant-Mode Mismatch problems identified in the analysis of top-k distillation.

title: Evaluating Token Probabilities as Confidence Estimators in Human Behavior Simulations: A Case Study in Luxembourgish Next Like Prediction
comment: 12 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Accepted to 11th Workshop on Natural User-generated Text (W-NUT) at EMNLP 2026, Budapest, Hungary
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, their operational validity is typically assessed through accuracy alone, implicitly treating human behavior as deterministic. We argue that on noisy digital trace data, a model's performance depends not only on predicting the correct outcome but on its calibration. We present a case study testing whether the token probabilities of open-weight LLMs can serve as confidence estimates in a Next Like Prediction task: predicting how a user of the Luxembourgish news platform this http URL rates a comment, conditioned on their prior interactions. Evaluating Ministral 3 (3B, 8B), we find that, with in-context learning only, the tested models are overconfident and are outperformed on accuracy and calibration by a simple statistical baseline. Accuracy and calibration do not move together: scaling from 3B to 8B improves accuracy while degrading calibration, and longer behavioral histories raise accuracy while confidence declines. Task-specific supervised fine-tuning acts as an effective calibration intervention, reducing Expected Calibration Error from 0.2 to 0.006 while improving accuracy from 0.536 to 0.758. We conclude that confidence estimation should be evaluated alongside accuracy to improve validity when using LLM-based agents.

AI.tldr: In-context open-weight LLMs are overconfident when predicting Luxembourgish comment ratings and are beaten on accuracy and calibration by a simple statistical baseline; task-specific fine-tuning fixes most of the calibration gap.
AI.motivation: LLM-based simulations of human behavior are usually validated by accuracy alone, which implicitly treats behavior as deterministic, whereas noisy digital trace data calls for well-calibrated confidence.
AI.method: Token probabilities of Ministral 3 (3B and 8B) serve as confidence estimates for predicting how a user of a Luxembourgish news platform rates a comment, conditioned on their prior interactions, and the models are compared with a simple statistical baseline.
AI.result: Scaling from 3B to 8B improves accuracy but degrades calibration, and longer behavioral histories raise accuracy while confidence declines; supervised fine-tuning reduces Expected Calibration Error from 0.2 to 0.006 while improving accuracy from 0.536 to 0.758.
AI.conclusion: Confidence estimation should be evaluated alongside accuracy to improve the validity of LLM-based agents that simulate human behavior.

title: Extending Reasoning in Typed Decision Models via Looping
summary: Typed decision models choose among a fixed set of answer options in a single forward pass, so unlike generative language models they cannot spend more test-time compute on hard inputs by generating more tokens. Looping a block of layers offers this compute in latent space without adding parameters, but prior work found no gain from loops retrofitted into conventionally pretrained models. We show that such loops help when trained together with the decision model. Our method, RELOAD (retrofitted loops for adaptive decisions), fine-tunes a pretrained encoder or decoder with a damped loop over its middle block and a lightweight controller picks the number of passes adaptively for each input. Across six models from 0.4B to 4B parameters, looping improves both accuracy and calibration, mostly on problems that need longer chains of reasoning than any seen in training, where encoders gain up to 23 points. Neither matched training compute nor more data closes this gap, and separate layers for each pass come close only with nearly twice the parameters. The controller keeps most of the gain at about three quarters of the compute.

AI.tldr: RELOAD trains a looped middle block jointly with a typed decision model and an adaptive controller, improving accuracy and calibration without adding parameters.
AI.motivation: Typed decision models pick one of fixed options in a single forward pass, so they cannot spend more test-time compute by generating tokens, and loops retrofitted onto conventionally pretrained models previously gave no gain.
AI.method: A pretrained encoder or decoder is fine-tuned with a damped loop over its middle block, and a lightweight controller picks the number of passes adaptively for each input.
AI.result: Across six models from 0.4B to 4B parameters, looping improves accuracy and calibration, mostly on problems needing longer reasoning chains than seen in training, where encoders gain up to 23 points; matched training compute and more data do not close the gap, and separate layers per pass come close only with nearly twice the parameters; the controller keeps most of the gain at about three quarters of the compute.
AI.conclusion: Training loops together with the decision model makes latent test-time compute useful for typed decisions.

title: Automated Video-to-QA Pipeline: End-to-End Question Generation and Verification Using Large Language Models
summary: The exponential growth of educational and informational video content on platforms like YouTube presents a challenge for efficient knowledge retrieval and assessment. This paper proposes an end-to-end automated pipeline for extracting structured summaries and generating high-fidelity Question-Answer (QA) pairs from video streams. The framework integrates a cascade of state-of-the-art models: audio extraction is handled via FFmpeg, followed by automatic speech recognition (ASR) using Whisper (A library in Python) to generate accurate transcripts. Due to the token constraints of Large Language Models (LLMs), transcripts are segmented and summarized using Facebook's BART. A key innovation of this work is a Self-Verification and Fine-Tuning Loop. We utilize meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8BInstruct to generate candidate QA pairs from transcript chunks, which are then fed back into the model to rigorously assess their relevance and importance. Only verified, high-quality pairs are retained to construct a synthetic dataset. This dataset is subsequently used to fine-tune the Llama model using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), resulting in a specialized model capable of generating domain-aligned assessment questions. This approach demonstrates a scalable method for creating self-improving educational tools without the need for manual data annotation. The proposed model can be downloaded from Kaggle with all the codes from GitHub.

AI.tldr: An end-to-end pipeline turns videos into transcripts, summaries and QA pairs, with a self-verification loop that filters Llama-generated pairs before LoRA fine-tuning the model on them.
AI.motivation: Educational and informational video is hard to search and assess efficiently, and building assessment material normally requires manual annotation.
AI.method: FFmpeg extracts audio, Whisper produces transcripts, BART summarizes transcript chunks, and meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8BInstruct generates candidate QA pairs that the same model verifies for relevance and importance; only verified pairs are used to fine-tune the model with LoRA.
AI.result: The abstract describes the pipeline and claims a scalable method, but reports no quantitative evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The approach is presented as a scalable way to create self-improving educational tools without manual annotation, with the model and code released on Kaggle and GitHub.

title: Bridging Structure and Semantics: Knowledge Graph Verification via Triple-to-Text Alignment
summary: Semantic accuracy is an important dimension of knowledge graph quality. Graph-based scoring methods exploit relational structure, while textual representations allow classifiers to draw on knowledge encoded by pre-trained language models (PLMs). We present GenVer, a generative verifier that scores triples using both their serialized form and generated natural language representations (NLRs). A triple-text alignment procedure selects training pairs for a sequence-to-sequence generator; a BERT-based classifier then combines features from each triple and its generated NLR. On four FactFB variants, constructed from FB15k using perturbed negative triples, GenVer obtains the highest classification accuracy among the evaluated baselines, ranging from 88.56% to 91.52%. The experiments suggest that generated representations can help triple classification, while the case analysis also exposes semantic drift and high-confidence errors.

AI.tldr: GenVer verifies knowledge graph triples by combining their serialized form with generated natural language representations, reaching 88.56% to 91.52% accuracy on four FactFB variants.
AI.motivation: Graph-based scoring exploits relational structure while textual representations let classifiers draw on knowledge encoded in pretrained language models, and the two had not been combined for triple verification.
AI.method: A triple-text alignment procedure selects training pairs for a sequence-to-sequence generator that produces natural language representations, and a BERT-based classifier combines features from each triple and its generated representation.
AI.result: On four FactFB variants built from FB15k with perturbed negative triples, GenVer obtains the highest classification accuracy among the evaluated baselines, from 88.56% to 91.52%; case analysis exposes semantic drift and high-confidence errors.
AI.conclusion: Generated representations can help triple classification, although they can introduce semantic drift and confident errors.

title: Dataset Collection and Fine-Tuning of NLLB for German--English Translation
summary: This paper describes the curation of a high-quality parallel corpus from OPUS Books and the fine-tuning of Meta's NLLB-200 models for German--English translation. We detail a dataset extraction pipeline that filters 45k raw OPUS sentence pairs to 25k high-quality examples through encoding validation, length filtering, language identification, deduplication, and quality scoring. We present a reproducible fine-tuning methodology optimized for consumer GPUs using mixed precision, gradient accumulation, and gradient checkpointing. Our fine-tuned NLLB-600M model achieves statistically significant improvements (+3.4 BLEU, +2.6 chrF++, -3.2 TER) over the base model on literary and technical German-English translation. We demonstrate practical deployment by integrating the fine-tuned model into LinguaHaru, an existing open-source document translation system, achieving format-preserving translation across PDF and Office documents. All dataset preparation scripts, training code, and evaluation tools are provided for reproducibility. The fine-tuned model is available at HuggingFace.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning NLLB-600M on a curated OPUS Books German-English corpus gives significant gains over the base model, and the model is integrated into LinguaHaru for format-preserving document translation.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses building a high-quality parallel corpus for German-English literary and technical translation and fine-tuning NLLB-200 models on consumer GPUs.
AI.method: A pipeline filters 45k raw OPUS sentence pairs to 25k through encoding validation, length filtering, language identification, deduplication and quality scoring, then fine-tunes NLLB-200 models with mixed precision, gradient accumulation and gradient checkpointing.
AI.result: The fine-tuned NLLB-600M improves on the base model by +3.4 BLEU, +2.6 chrF++ and -3.2 TER on literary and technical German-English translation, with statistical significance.
AI.conclusion: The model is deployed in LinguaHaru for format-preserving translation of PDF and Office documents, and all dataset scripts, training code and evaluation tools are provided for reproducibility.

title: Decodability Is Not Validity: Evaluating Nuisance Sensitivity in Language Model Concept Probes
comment: 4 pages + appendix; code and data: this https URL
summary: Two concept probes can be equally accurate at predicting a concept from a language model's hidden states while their scores contain different mixtures of the target concept and a correlated nuisance attribute. In four target--nuisance settings (two aspect sentiments in CEBaB; occupation and gender in BiasBios; Amazon review sentiment with negation, and with first-person framing), two LLMs, and a population of concept extractors, we compare decodability with discriminant evidence: the score's dependence on the nuisance at fixed target, and its response to input edits intended to change only the nuisance, filtered by two LLM judges and compared against placebo edits. Under correlated training data, extractors that are statistically equivalent in held-out AUROC differ up to several-fold in nuisance sensitivity in three of the four settings, and decodability is not a reliable proxy for it: their rank correlation changes sign across settings. The effect follows the probe's training data, not the nuisance's natural association with the target: first-person framing, unrelated to sentiment in natural reviews, is absorbed at least as much as negation, which co-occurs with negative sentiment, and decorrelated training removes the systematic effect. Selecting extractors with nuisance-aware development diagnostics, which need nuisance labels but no counterfactuals, lowers counterfactual nuisance sensitivity wherever the default choice is sensitive, at a small accuracy cost. Concept measurements should be validated, not just decoded.

AI.tldr: Concept probes with equal held-out AUROC can differ several-fold in sensitivity to a correlated nuisance attribute, so decodability alone does not validate a concept measurement.
AI.motivation: Decodability is the usual criterion for concept probes, but their scores can mix the target concept with a correlated nuisance attribute, which accuracy does not reveal.
AI.method: Across four target-nuisance settings, two LLMs and a population of concept extractors, decodability is compared with counterfactual nuisance sensitivity measured from input edits that target only the nuisance, filtered by two LLM judges and compared against placebo edits, alongside nuisance-aware development diagnostics.
AI.result: Extractors that are statistically equivalent in held-out AUROC differ up to several-fold in nuisance sensitivity in three of four settings, and their rank correlation with decodability changes sign across settings; selecting extractors with nuisance-aware diagnostics lowers counterfactual sensitivity at a small accuracy cost.
AI.conclusion: Concept measurements should be validated, not just decoded, and the nuisance sensitivity follows the probe's training data rather than the nuisance's natural association with the target.

title: Different Corpora, Different Skills? A Paired Study of Small Language Models
comment: Published in the Proceedings of the Second BabyLM Workshop (EMNLP 2026). 13 pages
summary: Small language models are often trained under tight data budgets, where the choice of pretraining corpus may matter as much as model size or training recipe. We compare two contrasting corpora at matched 10-million- and 37-million-word budgets: the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica and the BabyLM 2026 strict pretraining corpus. For each corpus, we train teacher models, distilled 58-million-parameter Baby-Llama students, and no-distillation student ablations, using the same model families, training recipes, and evaluation protocol across corpora. Across BLiMP, BLiMP Supplement, EWoK, Entity Tracking, and COMPS, the corpora produce different skill profiles rather than a single quality ranking. BabyLM 2026 is consistently stronger on linguistic acceptability benchmarks, while Britannica is often stronger on Entity Tracking, a synthetic state-tracking task. The contrast appears across teacher and student models and at both budgets, with the cleanest cross-seed replication in the distilled student comparison. Targeted controls show that the central contrast persists after matching training exposure and at a longer diagnostic context; direct teacher ensembling also does not reproduce the 10M Britannica student's Entity Tracking behavior. Entity Tracking magnitudes nevertheless remain sensitive to training dynamics. For this corpus pair, corpus choice can therefore produce different relative skill profiles at small scale, motivating multi-benchmark evaluation when comparing pretraining data.

AI.tldr: Small language models trained at matched budgets on the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica and on the BabyLM 2026 strict corpus show different skill profiles: BabyLM is stronger on linguistic acceptability and Britannica on Entity Tracking.
AI.motivation: Under tight data budgets the pretraining corpus may matter as much as model size or training recipe, and corpora are rarely compared on multi-skill profiles.
AI.method: Teacher models, distilled 58M-parameter Baby-Llama students and no-distillation ablations are trained on the two corpora at 10M and 37M words, with the same model families, recipes and evaluation protocol across BLiMP, BLiMP Supplement, EWoK, Entity Tracking and COMPS.
AI.result: BabyLM 2026 is consistently stronger on linguistic acceptability benchmarks and Britannica is often stronger on Entity Tracking, a contrast that appears across teachers and students at both budgets; it persists after matching training exposure and at a longer diagnostic context, and direct teacher ensembling does not reproduce the 10M Britannica student's Entity Tracking behavior.
AI.conclusion: Corpus choice produces different relative skill profiles at small scale, which motivates multi-benchmark evaluation when comparing pretraining data, although Entity Tracking magnitudes remain sensitive to training dynamics.

title: Axis-LoRA: Probing and Adapting Embedding Models for Personal-Memory Retrieval
summary: As LLMs are increasingly asked questions about a user's personal experiences, retrieval must distinguish memories by time, place, person, and event. Current personal-memory pipelines rely on frozen dense embedding models to embed memories for retrieval, but we find that these models do not capture the four axes well. Swapping a memory's date or place barely shifts its embedding, and a trained projection on top of the frozen embedding does not recover the missing signal. The problem lives inside the model, where each axis is encoded by a distinct attention-head pattern. Guided by these findings, we propose Axis-LoRA, a per-axis adapter that places four LoRA branches inside the embedding model and combines them via a per-query gate. Across three standard embedding models evaluated on LongMemEval, ATM-Bench, and LoCoMo, Axis-LoRA improves 4-benchmark mean R@10 by $+1.28$ to $+1.56$~pp while training only a small fraction of the base parameters on a small axis-counterfactual training set. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Axis-LoRA adds four per-axis LoRA branches, combined by a per-query gate, to embedding models to improve personal-memory retrieval across time, place, person and event.
AI.motivation: Frozen dense embedding models barely shift when a memory's date or place is swapped, and a trained projection on top of the frozen embedding does not recover the missing signal.
AI.method: Each axis is encoded by a distinct attention-head pattern inside the embedding model, so four LoRA branches are placed there and combined through a per-query gate, trained on a small axis-counterfactual set.
AI.result: Across three standard embedding models evaluated on LongMemEval, ATM-Bench and LoCoMo, the 4-benchmark mean R@10 improves by +1.28 to +1.56 percentage points while training only a small fraction of the base parameters.
AI.conclusion: Adapting the internal attention structure of embedding models to individual memory axes is a practical route to better personal-memory retrieval; code is released.

title: Towards Foundation Decision Models: Drex
comment: 51 pages, 13 figures, 25 tables. Models and code: this https URL
summary: Autoregressive approaches with large language models, such as long chain-of-thought reasoning, have become the default for new AI applications because they reach higher accuracy on a wide range of tasks. In production, however, they give inconsistent answers, require parsing of outputs, and add cost and latency. Decision models address this: given a question and a set of options supplied by the user, they return a probability distribution over the options without autoregressive decoding. We present Drex, a family of four open decision models with 8B (DLM), 9B (v1.5), 35B with 3B active (v2.0), and 27B (Max) parameters. Each request consists of a state (a document, record, or agent context, optionally with images) and questions about it, each asking for a choice among options, a yes/no judgment, or a score on an ordered scale. Training combines supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback (RLAF), plus vision tuning for Max. Ablations show that RLAF improves accuracy and that consistency losses improve robustness to option order. On Decision Index 0.4.1, Max sets a new state of the art among the decision models we compare (67.52 on the public suite vs. 60.70 for Jev 1.14.0). On Decision Bench v4, it is statistically tied with d3-turbo and GPT-6 Sol and trails Claude Opus 5.5 by 1.6 points, and it has the highest accuracy among decision models on DecideBench. Max answers a typical request in 183 ms, against about 2.0 s for GPT-6 Sol and 3.5 s for Claude Opus 5.5, and its outputs are stable under option reordering. All four models are open source: this https URL

AI.tldr: Drex is a family of four open decision models that return probability distributions over options without autoregressive decoding; the 27B Max model sets a new state of the art among the decision models compared.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive LLM reasoning gives inconsistent answers in production, requires output parsing, and adds cost and latency, whereas decision models can return option distributions directly.
AI.method: Four models with 8B (DLM), 9B (v1.5), 35B with 3B active (v2.0) and 27B (Max) parameters are trained with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback (RLAF), with vision tuning for Max and consistency losses for robustness to option order.
AI.result: Max scores 67.52 on the public suite of Decision Index 0.4.1 against 60.70 for Jev 1.14.0; on Decision Bench v4 it is statistically tied with d3-turbo and GPT-6 Sol and trails Claude Opus 5.5 by 1.6 points; it answers a typical request in 183 ms, against about 2.0 s for GPT-6 Sol and 3.5 s for Claude Opus 5.5.
AI.conclusion: Decision models can approach large autoregressive models on decision tasks at much lower latency, with outputs stable under option reordering, and all four models are open source.

title: CORE: Coarse-to-Fine Search with Context Management for Deep Research
summary: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent's context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE, a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus-CM), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

AI.tldr: CORE is a training-free harness for deep research agents that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. It reports state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall in closed-search comparisons against the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses.
AI.motivation: Search works best over long passages, which give reliable semantic matching, but every returned observation stays in the agent's context, so evidence must be short. Existing harnesses face this trade-off.
AI.method: Passages are retrieved with a dense retriever, and token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker are reused to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets.
AI.result: Across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus-CM), CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall, on corpora containing up to 553M documents.
AI.conclusion: Coarse-to-fine retrieval with context management gives agents long-passage matching reliability with short-evidence context cost, without any training.

title: Do Recommenders Need to Think in Words? Latent Reasoning for Efficient LLM-Based Recommendation
comment: Accepted at CIKM 2026 (Short Paper). 5 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables
summary: LLM-based recommender systems increasingly generate chain-of-thought (CoT) text before each item prediction to activate the LLM's reasoning capacity, costing tens to hundreds of extra tokens per recommendation at inference. We ask whether inference-time reasoning artifacts (textual or latent) can be replaced by training-time supervision alone, without loss of accuracy. We propose LatentRec, a framework for LLM-based generative recommendation that replaces inference-time reasoning artifacts with training-time per-step head supervision. LatentRec has three components. A 2.5M-parameter Continuous Thought Module iterates K latent reasoning steps over the LLM's hidden state during training. Soft Token Selection bridges the ~14x norm gap between hidden states and input embeddings. A Per-step Reasoning Loss (PRL) supervises every intermediate state through the LLM's prediction head against the first token of the target Semantic ID. The trained LLM retains this accuracy without the module at inference, so the module can be discarded at deployment. On three Amazon benchmarks, LatentRec improves HR@10 by 4.0-5.0% (relative) over a CoT-distilled baseline at 18.3x lower latency (batch=1). Per-step training supervision consistently improves accuracy across three datasets, paid once at training rather than at every recommendation.

AI.tldr: LatentRec replaces inference-time chain-of-thought in LLM-based recommendation with training-time latent reasoning supervision, so the reasoning module can be discarded at deployment. On three Amazon benchmarks it improves HR@10 by 4.0-5.0% (relative) over a CoT-distilled baseline at 18.3x lower latency with batch size 1.
AI.motivation: LLM recommenders generate chain-of-thought text before each item prediction, costing tens to hundreds of extra tokens per recommendation at inference. The paper asks whether such inference-time reasoning artifacts can be replaced by training-time supervision alone without losing accuracy.
AI.method: A 2.5M-parameter Continuous Thought Module iterates K latent reasoning steps over the LLM hidden state during training. Soft Token Selection bridges the roughly 14x norm gap between hidden states and input embeddings. A Per-step Reasoning Loss supervises every intermediate state through the LLM prediction head against the first token of the target Semantic ID.
AI.result: On three Amazon benchmarks, LatentRec improves HR@10 by 4.0-5.0% (relative) over a CoT-distilled baseline at 18.3x lower latency (batch=1). Per-step training supervision consistently improves accuracy across the three datasets.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning can be moved from inference to training: the trained LLM keeps its accuracy without the module, so the cost is paid once at training rather than at every recommendation.

title: AraEngage: Interpretable Linguistic Correlates of Engagement in Arabic Facebook News
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables. To appear in ArabicNLP 2026
summary: Engagement features developed for English are routinely applied to Arabic, but unvocalized Arabic changes what a lexical feature measures. We introduce AraEngage, a query-defined sample of 10,000 public Arabic Facebook news posts from 2,451 pages in 57 countries (2023-2024) that pairs engagement counts with interpretable linguistic features. We use it to examine which interpretable Arabic indicators are associated with follower-normalized engagement, and how far those associations can be trusted given publisher context, the definition of engagement, and lexical ambiguity. Religious expressions, message length, sentence length, and lexical density are the leading correlates in a Random Forest model ($R^2$ = 0.38 on a post-level split) interpreted with SHAP. Unlike English news, positive sentiment is associated with higher engagement in this Arabic news sample. Message length shows a length paradox: unadjusted raw engagement is highest for long posts, whereas the model's attributions for follower-normalized engagement favor short posts. A linguistic audit identifies why standard lexicon features are fragile in unvocalized Arabic: imperative lists contain homographs such as the form read as "express!" that is also the frequent preposition "via", hedge lists conflate the possibility marker qad + imperfect ("may") with the emphatic qad + perfect ("has indeed"), and religious lists mix devotional formulas with place names in political news. These are plausible sources of measurement error that may attenuate the near-zero associations of imperatives and hedges. All findings are observational associations with operationalized indicators. We release the derived linguistic features, engagement counts, refined lexicons, and analysis code; raw posts are not redistributed, in line with CrowdTangle terms.

AI.tldr: AraEngage is a dataset of 10,000 Arabic Facebook news posts paired with engagement counts and interpretable linguistic features. A Random Forest with SHAP identifies religious expressions, message length, sentence length and lexical density as leading correlates of follower-normalized engagement, and positive sentiment as associated with higher engagement, unlike English news.
AI.motivation: English engagement features are routinely applied to Arabic, but unvocalized Arabic changes what a lexical feature measures, so it is unclear which interpretable indicators can be trusted for engagement.
AI.method: A query-defined sample of 10,000 public Arabic Facebook news posts from 2,451 pages in 57 countries (2023-2024). A Random Forest model on interpretable linguistic features is interpreted with SHAP, alongside a linguistic audit of standard lexicon features for homographs and ambiguous markers.
AI.result: The Random Forest reaches R2 of 0.38 on a post-level split. Raw engagement is highest for long posts, while the model's attributions for follower-normalized engagement favor short posts. The audit finds that imperative and hedge lists contain homographs or conflated markers, and that religious lists mix devotional formulas with place names.
AI.conclusion: Standard lexicon features are fragile in unvocalized Arabic and may cause measurement error that attenuates some near-zero associations. All findings are observational, and the derived features, counts, refined lexicons and analysis code are released while raw posts are withheld under CrowdTangle terms.

title: CardioLM: A multilingual suite of small language models for the cardiology domain
comment: 91 pages, 7 figures, 33 tables (9 in the main text, 23 in Appendix A, and 1 in Appendix B)
summary: Background: Cardiovascular care generates large volumes of clinical free-text documentation in local languages. However, clinical natural language processing (NLP) resources remain concentrated in English, and no existing benchmark is cardiology-specific, multilingual, and broad in entity coverage. Methods: We present two contributions. The first is CardioCCC, a corpus of 508 cardiology case reports originally published in Spanish and extended to Czech, Dutch, English, Italian, Romanian, and Swedish through machine translation, annotation projection, and clinician review, with annotations covering diseases, symptoms, procedures, and medications. The second is CardioLM, comprising CardioBERTa, a set of language-specific encoders obtained by continued pretraining on cardiology and biomedical corpora, and CardioNER, a set of named entity recognition (NER) models fine-tuned on CardioCCC. Results: Cardiology-specific pretraining reduced pseudo-perplexity by up to a factor of eight, yet changed strict span-level F1 by at most 0.04, with benefits concentrated in languages whose backbones lacked biomedical coverage. The jointly trained multilingual XLM-RoBERTa-large models achieved the best strict F1 in nearly every language and entity type, exceeding the strongest monolingual system by up to 0.13 F1. A large share of residual errors concerned boundary detection: relaxed matching recovered 0.10-0.23 F1 for disease, procedure, and symptom, but only 0.01-0.07 for medication. Clinicians rated CardioNER well above a rule- and dictionary-based baseline, with the mean rating across entity types rising from 26% to 73%. Conclusions: Specialty-specific pretraining is not the decisive factor for downstream entity recognition, whereas multilingual joint training yields the strongest results in nearly all settings and a simpler deployment path for multi-country clinical information extraction.

AI.tldr: CardioLM is a suite of cardiology-specific multilingual models: CardioCCC, an annotated corpus of 508 cardiology case reports in seven languages, and CardioNER, NER models fine-tuned on it. Multilingual XLM-RoBERTa-large gives the best strict F1 in nearly every language and entity type, while cardiology-specific pretraining is not the decisive factor.
AI.motivation: Clinical NLP resources are concentrated in English, and no existing benchmark is cardiology-specific, multilingual and broad in entity coverage.
AI.method: CardioCCC, 508 cardiology case reports originally in Spanish and extended to six other languages through machine translation, annotation projection and clinician review, annotated for diseases, symptoms, procedures and medications. CardioBERTa is a set of language-specific encoders continually pretrained on cardiology and biomedical corpora. CardioNER is a set of NER models fine-tuned on CardioCCC.
AI.result: Cardiology pretraining reduced pseudo-perplexity by up to a factor of eight but changed strict span-level F1 by at most 0.04. The jointly trained XLM-RoBERTa-large achieved the best strict F1 in nearly every language and entity type, exceeding the strongest monolingual system by up to 0.13 F1. Relaxed matching recovered 0.10-0.23 F1 for disease, procedure and symptom but only 0.01-0.07 for medication. Clinicians rated CardioNER well above a rule- and dictionary-based baseline, with mean ratings rising from 26% to 73%.
AI.conclusion: Specialty-specific pretraining is not the decisive factor for downstream entity recognition, whereas multilingual joint training yields the strongest results and a simpler deployment path for multi-country clinical information extraction.

title: Beyond the Keyword: A Human-Annotated Benchmark for Arabic Anxiety-Related Discourse
summary: Keyword retrieval returns expressions of personal anxiety together with many other uses of anxiety-related language. We present a benchmark of 1,000 Arabic Twitter/X posts retrieved with the keyword qalaq ("anxiety/worry") and annotated for six discourse functions. Two native Arabic-speaking annotators labeled every post independently, reaching 51.1% raw agreement (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.378$). We then reviewed all 489 disagreements and all 511 agreements under the same guidelines. The review changed 120 of the agreed labels (23.5%), which shows that agreements need auditing as well as disagreements. The final labels form a consensus reference; on a random sample of 200 posts, an additional annotator agreed with it on 60.5% of posts ($\kappa = 0.517$). Against this reference, Fanar-C-2-27B reaches 79.8% accuracy and macro-F1 0.784 ($\kappa = 0.749$). Its errors concentrate in the residual category (41.1% of errors; precision 0.905, recall 0.447), whose definition is internally inconsistent in the executed prompt, so the low recall cannot be attributed to the model alone. Sociopolitical Anxiety (27.1%) outnumbers Personal Emotional Expression (22.0%); these are assignment proportions in the sample, not estimates of prevalence or retrieval precision. We release the guidelines, a residual-subtype scheme, a fixed data split, label provenance, and evaluation code.

AI.tldr: The paper releases a benchmark of 1,000 Arabic Twitter/X posts retrieved with the keyword qalaq ("anxiety/worry") and annotated for six discourse functions. Fanar-C-2-27B reaches 79.8% accuracy and macro-F1 0.784 against the consensus reference, with most errors in the residual category.
AI.motivation: Keyword retrieval returns expressions of personal anxiety together with many other uses of anxiety-related language, so a reliable labelled reference for discourse function is needed.
AI.method: Two native Arabic-speaking annotators labelled every post independently (raw agreement 51.1%, Cohen's kappa 0.378). The team then reviewed all 489 disagreements and all 511 agreements under the same guidelines, changing 120 agreed labels, and the final labels form a consensus reference.
AI.result: On a random sample of 200 posts, an additional annotator agreed with the consensus on 60.5% (kappa 0.517). Fanar-C-2-27B reaches 79.8% accuracy and macro-F1 0.784 (kappa 0.749). Its errors concentrate in the residual category (41.1% of errors; precision 0.905, recall 0.447), whose definition is internally inconsistent in the executed prompt.
AI.conclusion: Agreements need auditing as well as disagreements, and the low residual recall cannot be attributed to the model alone given the inconsistent category definition. The guidelines, residual-subtype scheme, fixed data split, label provenance and evaluation code are released.

title: Compression Through a Context Lens: Evaluating Adaptation, Quantization, and Distillation in Arabic Legal LLMs
summary: Model compression can facilitate the deployment of large language models in resource-constrained legal settings, but its effects on domain-specific performance may depend on the evaluation protocol. We investigate this issue using ArabLegalEval, a Saudi Arabic legal benchmark, under both with-context and no-context evaluation. The former provides supporting legal passages, while the latter assesses performance without external context. Removing the context produces accuracy gaps of up to 27 percentage points for the base model. We examine three stages: domain adaptation, quantization, and knowledge distillation across FANAR-9B, JAIS-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B. Four-bit quantization reduces model memory by 64-71%, with changes in no-context MCQ accuracy ranging from -3.2 to +1.6 percentage points. Distillation produces more variable results, with accuracy generally declining as student size decreases. A Qwen2.5-7B student distilled from FANAR achieves 76.6% no-context accuracy, compared with 77.2% for its teacher. Our findings suggest that no-context evaluation provides a useful complement to context-supported testing when assessing the effects of adaptation and compression on Arabic legal language models.

AI.tldr: On ArabLegalEval, a Saudi Arabic legal benchmark, removing supporting context drops base-model accuracy by up to 27 percentage points. A Qwen2.5-7B student distilled from FANAR reaches 76.6% no-context accuracy, against 77.2% for its teacher.
AI.motivation: Model compression can help deploy LLMs in resource-constrained legal settings, but its effects on domain performance may depend on the evaluation protocol, and with-context testing alone may not reveal them.
AI.method: Domain adaptation, quantization and knowledge distillation are examined across FANAR-9B, JAIS-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, evaluated on ArabLegalEval under both with-context and no-context protocols.
AI.result: Removing context produces accuracy gaps of up to 27 percentage points for the base model. Four-bit quantization reduces memory by 64-71%, with no-context MCQ accuracy changes from -3.2 to +1.6 points. Distillation is more variable, with accuracy generally declining as student size decreases.
AI.conclusion: No-context evaluation is a useful complement to context-supported testing when assessing how adaptation and compression affect Arabic legal language models.

title: Automatic keyphrase extraction and annotation: modern theoretical approaches and practical solutions for text and speech
summary: The exponential growth of textual and audiovisual information has made the task of automatic keyphrase extraction (KE) increasingly significant. This article provides a comprehensive analysis of contemporary theoretical approaches and practical solutions for KE across both text and speech modalities. The primary contribution of this work is its systematic synthesis of these often-disparate research strands into a unified analytical framework, highlighting the evolution of the field from statistical methods towards large language models (LLMs) and end-to-end speech processing. We examine the stages of KE, the characteristics of keyphrases in written and spoken language, and terminological nuances. Various methods for automatic KE are discussed and analyzed in detail: statistical, hybrid, machine learning-based, and structural. The review dedicates substantial attention to emerging paradigms, including keyphrase generation using LLMs, and provides a detailed overview of methodologies and challenges in automatic corpus annotation. Furthermore, we specifically analyze current directions and inherent difficulties in KE for spoken language, comparing transcript based and end-to-end acoustic approaches. This synthesis leads us to conclude that the field is moving towards a more integrated, context-aware paradigm. Future progress will depend on addressing key challenges such as data scarcity for low-resource languages, effective multimodal fusion, and the nuanced evaluation of generative KE systems.

AI.tldr: This review surveys automatic keyphrase extraction across text and speech, synthesizing statistical, hybrid, machine learning and structural methods with LLM-based keyphrase generation. It concludes that the field is moving toward a more integrated, context-aware paradigm.
AI.motivation: Keyphrase extraction research for text and speech is spread across separate strands, so a unified analytical framework is needed.
AI.method: A review covering the stages of keyphrase extraction, the characteristics of keyphrases in written and spoken language, terminology, statistical, hybrid, machine learning and structural methods, LLM-based keyphrase generation, and corpus annotation. It compares transcript-based and end-to-end acoustic approaches for spoken language.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experimental numbers. It identifies data scarcity for low-resource languages, effective multimodal fusion and the nuanced evaluation of generative keyphrase systems as key open challenges.
AI.conclusion: The field is moving from statistical methods towards LLMs and end-to-end speech processing, and future progress depends on addressing these challenges.

title: Linguistic boundaries emerge from pressure-constrained processing dynamics
summary: Human cognition organizes continuous experience into bounded units while maintaining continuity across them. Linguistic elements are also organized into bounded structural units such as words and phrases, with sentence marking the final bound of a grammatical construction process. How do such boundaries emerge? We propose boundaries emerge from interacting demands to maintain unresolved dependencies, integrate completed relations, and update semantic context, with structural completion allowing but not determining closure. First, in a generative simulation without predefined boundary positions or constituent labels, these demands produced sentence-like segment-length distributions and distinct characteristic timescales, with structural completion allowing but not determining closure. Near boundaries, unresolved dependency load declined, integration cost peaked, and accumulated pressure reset. Then, we tested whether same demands predicted human listeners' boundary choices during comprehension. Listeners were more likely to mark boundaries with fewer unresolved dependencies, higher integration cost and semantic mismatch, and elevated preceding memory load, beyond syntactic and prosodic cues. Third, in naturalistic self-paced reading, sentence-final slowing coincided with declining memory load and increasing integration cost and semantic mismatch, broadly consistent with the simulation. Processing same narratives with a large language model revealed increased local intrinsic dimensionality and straighter hidden-state trajectories at sentence endings, followed by larger representational updates. Boundary explained additional variation in reading time and hidden-state geometry beyond processing demands, but considerably less in next-token surprisal. Together, these findings suggest linguistic boundaries emerge as discrete manifestations of transitions in continuous processing dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that linguistic boundaries emerge from interacting processing demands: maintaining unresolved dependencies, integrating completed relations and updating semantic context. A generative simulation, human boundary judgments, self-paced reading and LLM hidden-state analyses support this account.
AI.motivation: Words, phrases and sentences are usually treated as predefined units, so the question is how such discrete boundaries arise from continuous processing.
AI.method: A generative simulation without predefined boundary positions or constituent labels. Tests check whether the same demands predict listeners' boundary choices beyond syntactic and prosodic cues, whether they predict sentence-final slowing in naturalistic self-paced reading, and how they relate to LLM hidden-state geometry on the same narratives.
AI.result: The simulation produced sentence-like segment-length distributions and distinct characteristic timescales. Listeners were more likely to mark boundaries with fewer unresolved dependencies, higher integration cost, semantic mismatch and elevated memory load. At sentence endings the LLM showed higher local intrinsic dimensionality and straighter hidden-state trajectories, and boundaries explained variation beyond processing demands but considerably less in next-token surprisal.
AI.conclusion: Linguistic boundaries are discrete manifestations of transitions in continuous processing dynamics rather than predefined structural units.

title: Beyond K/V Caches: Cross-Model State Handoff in Hybrid Linear-Attention LLMs
summary: Production deployments often use different models to balance cost and quality through cascading, routing, and switching models during long conversations. Context accumulates across turns. Each switch requires the target to repeat prefill over this context. Existing methods transfer full-attention (FA) K/V caches across models. Hybrid linear-attention models also retain recurrent states (REC) and convolution histories (Conv). The interaction between Conv and REC complicates cross-model state transfer. Conv perturbations can change keys and values in recurrent layers and alter REC updates. Conv histories are overwritten, but changes in REC can still affect later outputs. More accurate REC reconstruction need not improve continuation. Building on this, we propose Hybrid State Transfer (HST) for all three state types. It uses structured REC maps and preserves history order during Conv alignment. We calibrate the adapters using the frozen target's outputs during continuation. FA cache map updates are merged offline. Across five benchmarks, Qwen3.5 4B$\rightarrow$27B and 9B$\rightarrow$27B achieve mean task retentions of 89.88% and 94.11%, respectively. With source caches already available, separate timing on synthetic 16K inputs yields handoff body speedups of $21.66\times$ and $21.91\times$.

AI.tldr: Hybrid State Transfer (HST) moves full-attention KV caches, recurrent states and convolution histories between hybrid linear-attention LLMs when a conversation switches models, avoiding repeated prefill. Qwen3.5 4B to 27B and 9B to 27B achieve mean task retentions of 89.88% and 94.11%, with handoff body speedups of about 21.7x on synthetic 16K inputs.
AI.motivation: Switching models during long conversations forces the target to re-prefill the accumulated context. Existing methods transfer only full-attention K/V caches, and the interaction between convolution histories and recurrent states complicates transfer for hybrid models.
AI.method: HST covers all three state types, using structured recurrent-state maps and order-preserving convolution-history alignment. Adapters are calibrated on the frozen target's outputs during continuation, and full-attention cache map updates are merged offline.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks, Qwen3.5 4B to 27B and 9B to 27B achieve mean task retentions of 89.88% and 94.11%. With source caches available, handoff body speedups on synthetic 16K inputs are 21.66x and 21.91x.
AI.conclusion: More accurate recurrent-state reconstruction does not by itself improve continuation, so state transfer should be calibrated against the target's behaviour. This points toward cheaper cross-model switching for hybrid models.

title: Knowing When to Teach: Learning from Teachable Prefixes in Multilingual Reasoning Distillation
summary: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) improves reasoning by training a student on its own reasoning, using the same model conditioned on reference solutions as a teacher. Applying OPSD to multilingual reasoning requires the teacher to provide useful feedback across languages, even when the student makes mistakes in intermediate steps. We observe a phenomenon we call Teacher Drift: as these mistakes accumulate, the teacher may follow the student's incorrect steps instead of correcting them. Our analysis shows that this shift tends to occur earlier in lower-resource languages. To account for these differences across languages, we propose Teachable On-Policy Self-Distillation (TOPSD), which determines where and whether teacher supervision should be applied to each reasoning trajectory. TOPSD uses teacher-student likelihood to estimate where drift begins and select a prefix for supervision. It then verifies whether the teacher can recover the correct answer from that prefix, applying distillation only to prefixes that pass verification. Experiments on multilingual mathematical reasoning across ten languages and three model scales show that TOPSD consistently outperforms conventional OPSD, particularly in low- and medium-resource languages.

AI.tldr: TOPSD is a teachable on-policy self-distillation method for multilingual reasoning. It uses teacher-student likelihood to find where drift begins, then applies teacher supervision only to prefixes from which the teacher can recover the correct answer, and it consistently outperforms conventional OPSD across ten languages and three model scales.
AI.motivation: OPSD requires the teacher to give useful feedback across languages, but Teacher Drift occurs when the teacher follows the student's accumulated mistakes instead of correcting them. This shift tends to occur earlier in lower-resource languages.
AI.method: Teachable On-Policy Self-Distillation decides where and whether teacher supervision applies to each trajectory. Teacher-student likelihood estimates where drift begins and selects a prefix. The teacher must then recover the correct answer from that prefix, and distillation is applied only to prefixes that pass verification.
AI.result: Experiments on multilingual mathematical reasoning across ten languages and three model scales show that TOPSD consistently outperforms conventional OPSD, particularly in low- and medium-resource languages.
AI.conclusion: Teacher supervision is more effective when applied selectively, by drift location and verifiability, rather than uniformly, and the benefit is largest for lower-resource languages.

title: Agent-R$^2$: Scaling Agents for Realistic Productivity Work via Real-Source Data Synthesis
summary: Large language models have made rapid progress in agentic reasoning and tool use, raising expectations for agents that can take over realistic productivity work from humans. However, current agents still struggle to finish such tasks, where success requires following long-horizon professional workflows, understanding heterogeneous file contexts, and producing usable deliverables under fine-grained requirements. A key bottleneck is the lack of scalable post-training data that reflects real work intent, authentic file environments, and deliverable-level evaluation. To close this gap, we introduce Agent-R$^2$, a $\textbf{r}$eal-source data synthesis framework that scales training data for $\textbf{r}$ealistic productivity work. Instead of relying on manually specified workflows or LLM-generated files, Agent-R$^2$ grounds synthesis throughout the pipeline in real occupational seeds, corpus-derived workflow evidence, and authentic web-sourced files. From 10k web-corpus candidates, Agent-R$^2$ distills 4k task instances that pair real multi-format attachments with fine-grained, deliverable-level rubrics. On this data, we train Agent-R$^2$-4B via supervised fine-tuning and rubric-based reinforcement learning, improving both end-to-end productivity performance and file-grounded reasoning. Trained on only 4k instances, Agent-R$^2$-4B surpasses Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 on both GDPval (51.0$\%$ vs. 48.0$\%$) and OfficeQA (14.8$\%$ vs. 13.8$\%$). Further analysis shows that Agent-R$^2$ mitigates shortcut behavior, where agents produce superficially plausible deliverables before sufficiently grounding, constructing, or verifying them, while promoting sustained exploration.

AI.tldr: Agent-R2 synthesizes post-training data for realistic productivity work from real occupational seeds, web-sourced files and rubrics, distilling 4k task instances from 10k candidates. Its 4B model, trained on those 4k instances, surpasses Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 on GDPval (51.0% vs 48.0%) and OfficeQA (14.8% vs 13.8%).
AI.motivation: Agents struggle to finish realistic productivity tasks, and current post-training data lacks real work intent, authentic file environments and deliverable-level evaluation. Manually specified workflows and LLM-generated files do not close this gap.
AI.method: Real-source data synthesis grounded in real occupational seeds, corpus-derived workflow evidence and authentic web-sourced files. The 4k tasks pair real multi-format attachments with fine-grained, deliverable-level rubrics. Agent-R2-4B is trained by supervised fine-tuning followed by rubric-based reinforcement learning.
AI.result: Agent-R2-4B surpasses Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 on GDPval (51.0% vs 48.0%) and OfficeQA (14.8% vs 13.8%) despite training on only 4k instances. Analysis shows reduced shortcut behavior, where agents produce plausible deliverables before grounding or verifying them, and more sustained exploration.
AI.conclusion: Grounding data synthesis in real work seeds and files can yield a small model that outperforms a much larger one on productivity tasks, while reducing shortcut behavior.

title: From Twisted Facts to Rogue Agents: Can LLMs Reliably Detect Multi-Dimensional Hallucinations?
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used for information access, content production, and agent-based task execution, but their outputs remain vulnerable to subtle, high-risk hallucinations. To systematically evaluate and advance post-generation hallucination detection, we introduce HaluCheck, a large-scale, bilingual benchmark comprising over 42k instances spanning both factual hallucinations in text and faithfulness hallucinations in agent trajectories. HaluCheck features fine-grained, multi-level annotations for detection, localization, and correction, covering different tasks and perturbation degrees. Experiments on fourteen LLMs reveal that, while models show basic sample-level detection ability, they struggle with fine-grained localization, correction, and agent hallucination detection. Further analysis demonstrates that thinking, web search, and supervised fine-tuning each offer partial improvements, but none fully solve the problem. HaluCheck thus provides a solid basis for benchmarking and diagnosing LLM reliability across text and agent scenarios.

AI.tldr: HaluCheck is a bilingual benchmark of over 42k instances for detecting multi-dimensional hallucinations in text and agent trajectories, with multi-level annotations for detection, localization and correction. Fourteen LLMs detect sample-level hallucinations but struggle with fine-grained localization, correction and agent hallucination detection.
AI.motivation: LLM outputs carry subtle, high-risk hallucinations, and post-generation detection needs systematic evaluation across both factual text and agent trajectories.
AI.method: HaluCheck spans factual hallucinations in text and faithfulness hallucinations in agent trajectories, covering different tasks and perturbation degrees, with fine-grained annotations for detection, localization and correction.
AI.result: Experiments on fourteen LLMs show basic sample-level detection ability but weak fine-grained localization, correction and agent hallucination detection. Thinking, web search and supervised fine-tuning each give partial improvements, but none fully solves the problem.
AI.conclusion: HaluCheck provides a basis for benchmarking and diagnosing LLM reliability across text and agent scenarios.

title: Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench: The First Agentic and Verifiable Benchmark for Mathematical Modeling
summary: Mathematical modeling turns an open-ended real-world problem into assumptions, a model, a solution, and a defended recommendation, and its answers matter only if they are both close to a credible reference and physically feasible; existing benchmarks either score solver fragments or grade reports with an LLM judge, leaving those numbers unchecked. We introduce TB-MathModel (the Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench), the first benchmark to make complete contest-style modeling problems agentic, verifiable, and terminal at once, over 18 real CUMCM and MCM problems (2023--2025). Each task ships the verbatim statement, official attachments, and figures in a containerized terminal; the agent returns one JSON artifact, scored on the numeric core of the final question against a reproduction of the Outstanding-award paper. Two design choices distinguish it: direction-aware, one-sided scoring, which never penalises beating the anchor, and two-layer feasibility verification---a programmatic gate over six decidable invariant forms plus 624 Lean~4 obligations---with a hard gate that zeroes infeasible answers. Each task is scored against a panel of human outstanding papers rather than one, so a model must be close to many accepted answers; across seven multimodal entries (three seeds each) the strongest reach a multi-reference O-Eval of 64.58\%, while the \$2.54 open model holds 59.81\% at $1/100$ the cost. TB-MathModel turns the numeric core of modeling into a reproducible, machine-checkable signal for measuring long-horizon modeling competence and for collecting agent trajectories. The source code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TB-MathModel is a benchmark of 18 real CUMCM and MCM modeling problems (2023-2025) run in containerized terminals, where agents return a JSON artifact scored against an Outstanding-award reference. The strongest of seven multimodal entries reach a multi-reference O-Eval of 64.58%, and a 2.54-dollar open model holds 59.81% at 1/100 the cost.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks either score solver fragments or grade full reports with an LLM judge, leaving numeric answers unchecked for closeness to a credible reference and for physical feasibility.
AI.method: Complete contest-style problems are made agentic, verifiable and terminal. The verbatim statement, attachments and figures sit in a container, and the agent returns one JSON artifact scored on the numeric core of the final question with direction-aware, one-sided scoring that never penalises beating the anchor. A two-layer feasibility check combines six decidable invariant forms and 624 Lean 4 obligations, with a hard gate that zeroes infeasible answers. Each task is scored against a panel of human outstanding papers.
AI.result: Across seven multimodal entries (three seeds each), the strongest reach a multi-reference O-Eval of 64.58%, while a 2.54-dollar open model holds 59.81% at 1/100 the cost.
AI.conclusion: TB-MathModel offers a reproducible, machine-checkable signal for measuring long-horizon modeling competence and for collecting agent trajectories.

title: Multimodal-SEA: Benchmarking AI Agent Security under Multimodal Social Engineering Attacks
summary: Personal AI agents face social engineering attacks supported by forged multimodal content, but existing evaluations mainly focus on text-based dialogue, leaving their intrinsic security under such attacks insufficiently studied. We introduce Multimodal-SEA, an interactive benchmark comprising 608 expert-designed tasks grounded in real-world fraud cases, covering 14 domains and 152 attack scenarios with prepared multimodal content. The tasks span four difficulty levels and reflect the distinct social and cultural contexts of Chinese and English environments. Agents inspect content, verify requests, and execute actions in simulated applications, with attack outcomes grounded in verifiable tool execution logs. To enable controlled red teaming of personal agents, we design a multimodal attack harness that integrates task information, attack progression control, and multimodal content construction to evaluate their intrinsic security against adaptive social engineering attacks in simulated environments. Evaluating seven widely used multimodal models across six dimensions reveals that all are vulnerable, with attack success rates of 7.1% to 34.5%. Adding multimodal content increases attack success from 19.9% to 29.2%, despite increased proactive verification coverage. Stronger safety instructions reduce attack success without improving recognition of deceptive multimodal content, while lower attack success rates for some models accompany excessive refusal of legitimate requests.

AI.tldr: Multimodal-SEA is an interactive benchmark of 608 tasks testing social engineering attacks on personal AI agents that use forged multimodal content. All seven evaluated multimodal models are vulnerable, with attack success rates of 7.1% to 34.5%, and adding multimodal content raises attack success from 19.9% to 29.2%.
AI.motivation: Personal agents face social engineering supported by forged multimodal content, but existing evaluations focus on text-based dialogue, leaving their security under such attacks insufficiently studied.
AI.method: 608 expert-designed tasks grounded in real fraud cases, covering 14 domains and 152 attack scenarios across four difficulty levels, with Chinese and English contexts. Agents inspect content, verify requests and execute actions in simulated applications, with outcomes checked against tool execution logs. A multimodal attack harness controls attack progression and constructs the multimodal content.
AI.result: Seven widely used multimodal models are all vulnerable across six dimensions, with attack success rates of 7.1% to 34.5%. Adding multimodal content raises attack success from 19.9% to 29.2% despite more proactive verification. Stronger safety instructions reduce attack success without improving recognition of deceptive content, and lower attack rates for some models come with excessive refusal of legitimate requests.
AI.conclusion: Personal agents remain weak against multimodal social engineering, and lower attack success can partly reflect over-refusal rather than better recognition of deception.

title: Measured Coupling for Parallel Decoding in Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion language models can write many tokens per step, but must choose which tokens are safe to commit together. Mean-field decoding penalizes pairs of positions whose predictions look alike. We replace this proxy with the coupling itself: how much committing one token changes the model's confidence at another. Cheap probes inside the main forward pass measure it, with no training or extra model, and it plugs into the same mean-field rule. On three models and four benchmarks, our method needs far fewer steps than mean-field decoding and is faster in most settings, also with a key-value cache, at an average accuracy cost of 1.1 points. Shuffling the couplings or replacing them with a uniform bonus loses this gain.

AI.tldr: A training-free decoder for diffusion language models measures the coupling between positions directly, how much committing one token changes the model's confidence at another, using cheap probes inside the main forward pass. It needs far fewer steps than mean-field decoding at an average accuracy cost of 1.1 points.
AI.motivation: Diffusion language models can commit many tokens per step but must choose which tokens are safe to commit together. Mean-field decoding uses a proxy that penalizes pairs of positions whose predictions look alike.
AI.method: The similarity proxy is replaced with the measured coupling itself, obtained from cheap probes inside the main forward pass, with no training or extra model. The measured coupling plugs into the same mean-field rule.
AI.result: On three models and four benchmarks, the method needs far fewer steps than mean-field decoding and is faster in most settings, including with a key-value cache, at an average accuracy cost of 1.1 points. Shuffling the couplings or replacing them with a uniform bonus loses the gain.
AI.conclusion: Measured inter-token coupling is a better basis than a similarity proxy for choosing which tokens to decode in parallel.

title: LLM-Assisted Label Noise Correction for EEG-Based Sleep Stage Classification
summary: Automatic sleep stage classification from electroencephalography (EEG) signals is a critical task in clinical sleep medicine. While deep learning models have shown promising results in this domain, their performance is fundamentally constrained by the quality of training labels, which human experts manually annotate and that are subject to inter-rater disagreement and systematic labeling errors. In this paper, we propose a novel LLM-assisted label-noise filtering pipeline that operates exclusively during training to identify and remove unreliable sleep-stage annotations before retraining the classifier. Specifically, TinySleepNet is first trained on the original dataset to extract per-epoch SoftMax confidence scores, then low-confidence epochs are submitted to LLaMA 3.1 along with their EEG spectral features and surrounding sequence context. The LLM evaluates each epoch against AASM sleep-scoring guidelines and assigns a verdict of RELIABLE or SUSPICIOUS. Suspicious epochs are removed from the training set, and TinySleepNet is retrained on the cleaned data. Evaluated on the Sleep-EDF Expanded dataset using 20-fold cross-validation, our method improves overall accuracy from 81.8% to 84.6% and Macro F1-score from 75.6% to 77.4%, with particularly notable gains in REM detection. Crucially, because the LLM operates only during training, the lightweight TinySleepNet architecture (1.3M parameters) is preserved at inference, making the proposed pipeline suitable for real-time, wearable sleep monitoring applications.

AI.tldr: An LLM (LLaMA 3.1) filters low-confidence sleep-stage labels during training only, removing suspicious epochs before retraining TinySleepNet. On Sleep-EDF Expanded under 20-fold cross-validation, accuracy rises from 81.8% to 84.6% and Macro F1 from 75.6% to 77.4%, with the 1.3M-parameter model unchanged at inference.
AI.motivation: EEG sleep-stage classifiers are limited by label quality, since expert annotations show inter-rater disagreement and systematic labeling errors.
AI.method: TinySleepNet is first trained on the original dataset to obtain per-epoch SoftMax confidences. Low-confidence epochs are sent to LLaMA 3.1 with their EEG spectral features and surrounding sequence context, and the LLM judges each against AASM sleep-scoring guidelines as RELIABLE or SUSPICIOUS. Suspicious epochs are removed and TinySleepNet is retrained on the cleaned data.
AI.result: Overall accuracy improves from 81.8% to 84.6% and Macro F1 from 75.6% to 77.4% under 20-fold cross-validation on Sleep-EDF Expanded, with particularly notable gains in REM detection.
AI.conclusion: Because the LLM operates only during training, the lightweight architecture is preserved at inference, which suits real-time wearable sleep monitoring.

title: Polarity Classification with Multitask Learning Syntax Augmentation
summary: Sentiment Analysis (SA) is a fundamental NLP task concerned with the identification and categorization of subjective information in text. While lexicon-based methods offer transparency, they often struggle with linguistic phenomena such as negation and intensification. Syntactic parsing has been integrated into SA pipelines to address this, but conventional parsers introduce significant computational overhead. Recent work shows that reformulating dependency parsing as a Sequence Labeling (SEL) task can improve efficiency. We propose and compare two strategies for integrating syntactic knowledge into a neural sentiment analysis model under unified Multi-Task Learning (MTL). The first, Standard-MTL, jointly learns dependency parsing (via sequence labeling) and sentiment polarity classification using a shared encoder with two task-specific heads. The second, Contrastive-MTL, provides implicit syntactic guidance through a contrastive auxiliary objective and a syntax-biased attention pooling mechanism, without requiring explicit label prediction. Both rely on syntactic annotations during training and eliminate need for hand-crafted compositional rules or external parsing at inference. We evaluate eleven datasets spanning seven languages---the MARC corpus (English, Spanish, French, German) and seven datasets from SemEval-2022 Task 10 (English, Spanish, Norwegian, Basque, Catalan)---using four established SEL encodings. With the relative encoding, Contrastive-MTL outperforms a syntax-naive baseline on 10 of 11 datasets and surpasses the external rule-based pipeline (SELSP) that parses at inference on all six datasets where the latter applies, while being 1.5--9$\times$ faster at evaluation. Standard-MTL is more dataset- and encoding-dependent. These results show implicit syntactic supervision during training can match or exceed explicit parsing at inference without computational overhead.

AI.tldr: Two multitask strategies inject syntax into neural sentiment analysis during training only. With the relative encoding, Contrastive-MTL beats a syntax-naive baseline on 10 of 11 datasets and is 1.5-9x faster at evaluation than the SELSP pipeline, which parses at inference.
AI.motivation: Syntactic parsing helps sentiment analysis with negation and intensification, but conventional parsers add significant computational overhead.
AI.method: Standard-MTL shares an encoder between dependency parsing, learned as sequence labeling, and polarity classification. Contrastive-MTL gives implicit syntactic guidance through a contrastive auxiliary objective and a syntax-biased attention pooling mechanism, without explicit label prediction. Both use syntactic annotations in training and need no hand-crafted rules or external parser at inference.
AI.result: On eleven datasets across seven languages (MARC and SemEval-2022 Task 10) with four SEL encodings, Contrastive-MTL outperforms the syntax-naive baseline on 10 of 11 datasets and surpasses SELSP on all six datasets where SELSP applies, while being 1.5-9x faster at evaluation. Standard-MTL is more dependent on dataset and encoding.
AI.conclusion: Implicit syntactic supervision during training can match or exceed explicit parsing at inference without computational overhead.

title: Cultural Adaptation within Repeated Social Interactions
summary: Much of human culture is tacit and is typically learned through situated social interaction.
