As LLMs are deployed as interactive agents across diverse communities, assessing their cultural competence demands moving beyond existing question-answering approaches, shifting from what they know to how they adapt. In this work, we broaden the scope of cultural adaptation in NLP by investigating whether LLMs can adapt through repeated interactions via a sandbox environment. By reframing cultural adaptation as a continuous process of norm assimilation through social interaction, our work demonstrates that memory mechanisms foster longitudinal learning across repeated interactions, facilitate transfer to different social settings, and enable multilingual norm assimilation across five languages. Together, our findings lay the groundwork for continuous, interaction-driven cultural adaptation in LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes cultural competence as adaptation: LLM agents in a sandbox interact repeatedly and assimilate social norms. Memory mechanisms support longitudinal learning, transfer across social settings and multilingual norm assimilation across five languages.
AI.motivation: Question-answering benchmarks measure what LLMs know about culture, not how they adapt through situated social interaction, which is how much of human culture is learned.
AI.method: A sandbox environment in which LLMs interact repeatedly, with memory mechanisms, framing cultural adaptation as continuous norm assimilation through social interaction. The setup is evaluated across social settings and five languages.
AI.result: The abstract reports qualitatively that memory mechanisms foster longitudinal learning across repeated interactions, facilitate transfer to different social settings, and enable multilingual norm assimilation across five languages. No numbers are given.
AI.conclusion: The findings lay the groundwork for continuous, interaction-driven cultural adaptation in LLMs.

title: SpecCTMC: Exact Speculative Simulation of Diffusion Language Model Continuous-Time Markov Chains
summary: Masked diffusion language models offer parallel text generation, but independently sampling multiple tokens can disrupt their dependencies and change the output distribution. Exact continuous-time sampling avoids this approximation, yet typically requires one sequential model evaluation per token. We introduce SpecCTMC, a training-free speculative sampler that reduces this sequential bottleneck without a separate draft model. SpecCTMC proposes successive token updates using previously computed model predictions, evaluates their intermediate states in parallel, and applies an exact acceptance-and-correction procedure. We prove that SpecCTMC preserves the joint distribution of event times, generation order, and token values of the underlying continuous-time Markov chain. It therefore introduces neither time-discretization error nor additional factorization error from parallel decoding. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B across five benchmarks demonstrate 1.73-4.38x fewer sequential model evaluations than direct continuous-time sampling, while preserving the reference sampling distribution. Our code is available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: SpecCTMC is a training-free speculative sampler for masked diffusion language models that exactly preserves the continuous-time Markov chain distribution. It cuts sequential model evaluations by 1.73-4.38x compared with direct continuous-time sampling, with no time-discretization error and no factorization error from parallel decoding.
AI.motivation: Parallel token sampling in masked diffusion language models can disrupt token dependencies and change the output distribution, while exact continuous-time sampling typically needs one sequential model evaluation per token.
AI.method: SpecCTMC proposes successive token updates from previously computed model predictions, evaluates the intermediate states in parallel, and applies an exact acceptance-and-correction procedure. No separate draft model is needed.
AI.result: The authors prove that SpecCTMC preserves the joint distribution of event times, generation order and token values. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B across five benchmarks, it needs 1.73-4.38x fewer sequential model evaluations than direct continuous-time sampling while preserving the reference sampling distribution.
AI.conclusion: Exact continuous-time sampling of diffusion language models can be accelerated substantially without approximation error.

title: MedGraph: Maintaining Patient State with Graph Memory for Long-Term Medical Dialogue
summary: LLM-based medical assistants that follow a patient across visits need a memory that keeps the patient's clinical state correct as it changes. We examine the errors of five memory systems on longitudinal medical dialogue and find three recurring causes: the retrieved evidence gives an outdated state, includes another person's health facts, or lacks a safety fact the answer depends on. We present MedGraph, a graph memory built for these three cases. Construction extracts dated facts from each session, attributes each fact to the person it describes, and links medication, diagnosis, and measurement records into chains that keep earlier states. Retrieval ranks the patient's chains as units, reads each chain at the time the question asks about, and adds the original dialogue text; a patient profile lists every recorded safety fact with every question. On MedMemoryBench, MedGraph has the highest overall accuracy with both a GPT and a Qwen backbone, 10.5 and 10.4 points above the strongest of five baselines, with efficient memory construction and answering in the GPT setting.

AI.tldr: MedGraph is a graph memory for long-term medical dialogue that extracts dated, person-attributed facts from each session and links medication, diagnosis and measurement records into state chains. It has the highest overall accuracy on MedMemoryBench with both GPT and Qwen backbones, 10.5 and 10.4 points above the strongest of five baselines.
AI.motivation: Memory systems for LLM medical assistants make three recurring errors on longitudinal dialogue: retrieved evidence gives an outdated state, includes another person's health facts, or lacks a safety fact the answer depends on.
AI.method: Construction extracts dated facts from each session, attributes each fact to the person it describes, and links medication, diagnosis and measurement records into chains that keep earlier states. Retrieval ranks a patient's chains as units, reads each chain at the time the question asks about, and adds the original dialogue text. A patient profile lists every recorded safety fact with every question.
AI.result: On MedMemoryBench, MedGraph has the highest overall accuracy with both GPT and Qwen backbones, 10.5 and 10.4 points above the strongest of five baselines, with efficient memory construction and answering in the GPT setting.
AI.conclusion: Targeting the three identified error causes with time-aware, person-attributed graph memory improves accuracy in longitudinal medical dialogue.

title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety
summary: Neural networks are likely to be among the most consequential artefacts in human history. As these systems become more capable and autonomous, their potential to cause societal harm also grows, making AI safety one of the defining challenges of our time. Yet we continue to build increasingly powerful systems without fully understanding how they work, how they will behave in unfamiliar situations, or how to reliably control them. Mechanistic interpretability offers a path towards understanding these systems by studying their internal representations and computations, with the aim of evaluating, predicting, and controlling behaviour. We survey mechanistic interpretability for AI safety in order to answer the question: Does understanding how models work actually make them safer? We place mechanistic interpretability in the broader context of interpretability research and compare its mechanistic evidence with behavioural evaluation. We introduce the foundations of mechanistic interpretability, including features, polysemanticity, transformer computation, and circuits, and survey methods for feature extraction and analysis, circuit discovery and causal verification, explaining intermediate representations in natural language, learning dynamics, and training-data attribution. Beyond surveying existing methods, we propose a unified framework for evaluating mechanistic interpretability claims and characterise six research orientations by their goals, assumptions, and trade-offs. Finally, we examine how mechanistic understanding can support AI safety, including knowledge editing, steering, and monitoring, and assess its limitations, failure modes, open problems, and relationship to behavioural safety measures. We also release a repository of code notebooks with worked examples that reproduce key findings from surveyed methods, allowing readers to build intuition through hands-on experimentation.

AI.tldr: The paper surveys mechanistic interpretability as a route to AI safety, asking whether understanding how models work makes them safer. It introduces foundations, reviews methods, proposes a unified framework for evaluating interpretability claims, and maps six research orientations.
AI.motivation: As neural networks grow more capable and autonomous, they are built without full understanding of how they work, how they behave in unfamiliar situations, or how to control them reliably. The paper positions mechanistic interpretability against broader interpretability research and behavioural evaluation.
AI.method: The survey covers features, polysemanticity, transformer computation and circuits, and methods for feature extraction, circuit discovery and causal verification, natural-language explanation of intermediate representations, learning dynamics and training-data attribution. It adds a unified framework for evaluating mechanistic claims, characterises six research orientations by goals, assumptions and trade-offs, and releases a repository of code notebooks reproducing key findings.
AI.result: The paper reports no new empirical numbers in the abstract. Its findings are the comparison of mechanistic evidence with behavioural evaluation and an assessment of how mechanistic understanding supports knowledge editing, steering and monitoring, including limitations, failure modes and open problems.
AI.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability can support safety through editing, steering and monitoring, but its benefits and limits must be assessed against behavioural safety measures; the released notebooks let readers test the surveyed methods hands-on.

title: Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes
comment: 11 pages, 6 tables. Model: this https URL ; code: this https URL ; archived release: this https URL
summary: Typed-decision models score options that the caller supplies at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model's developer does not control. We compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks; the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms. Holding questions fixed and varying only how eighteen routing labels are worded, we evaluate ten label vocabularies, produced by three separate processes and checked for overlap with the training data, with five candidates per question and, for eight of them, also with eighteen. On held-out vocabularies made of ordinary or borrowed words (English-derived jargon, office slang, department names), the augmented release is more accurate in every setting, by up to 0.24. Eleven of these fourteen gains survive a Holm correction (slang with eighteen candidates and descriptive sentences with five do not), and for jargon on all labels the label-level interval excludes zero in both settings. On abbreviations and opaque codes it gives no usable gain: on abbreviations it is not better, and worse on the clean slice, and on opaque codes both releases stay at or below chance once labels related to training options are removed. In most cells where accuracy rises, the risk-coverage area falls, but with eighteen candidates confident errors rise on jargon and slang. On two datasets neither release saw, accuracy moves by -8.4 and +5.6 points. We also report four evaluation hazards from comparing the two releases.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a later release of a 307M-parameter multilingual Russian cross-encoder, trained with label-wording augmentation, is more accurate on unfamiliar words such as jargon, slang and department names, but gives no usable gain on abbreviations or opaque codes.
AI.motivation: Typed-decision models score caller-supplied labels at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording the developer does not control. Existing evaluations do not show how label wording affects accuracy across different kinds of vocabulary.
AI.method: The authors compare two releases of Ru-Jev, a 307M-parameter model trained on thirteen Russian tasks, where the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms. They hold questions fixed, vary only the wording of eighteen routing labels across ten vocabularies from three processes, use five and eighteen candidates, and apply a Holm correction and label-level intervals.
AI.result: On held-out ordinary, borrowed and jargon vocabularies the augmented release is more accurate in every setting, by up to 0.24, and 11 of 14 gains survive the Holm correction. On abbreviations and opaque codes it gives no usable gain, and on two unseen datasets accuracy moves by -8.4 and +5.6 points. Confident errors rise on jargon and slang with eighteen candidates.
AI.conclusion: Label-wording augmentation helps a typed-decision encoder with unfamiliar words but not with abbreviations or codes, and its gains can come with more confident errors, so evaluation must test label wording directly.

title: Octopus: One Brain, Many Branches for Latent-KV Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems explore in parallel by spawning sub-agents with isolated context windows, whereas single-agent systems append every search and verification step into one growing trajectory. However, existing multi-agent frameworks duplicate prefix KV caches across branches, exchange findings by re-prefilling text summaries, and flatten or drop cross-branch dependencies during reinforcement learning (RL). We introduce Octopus, a single-model multi-agent RL framework in which all threads share one backbone and coordinate over a GPU-resident directed acyclic graph (DAG) of KV states through five primitives (fork, read_thread, wait_threads, rewind, commit). Octopus combines three co-designed mechanisms: (1) Zero-Copy Radix Forking, which spawns branches as $\mathcal{O}(1)$ cursor views over shared physical KV pages; (2) Attention-Only KV Mounting, which mounts a sibling thread's terminal KV blocks directly into full-attention layers while bypassing linear-recurrent states (Gated DeltaNet / Mamba-2), cutting off-task hijacking by $21\times$ ($57.9\% \to 2.7\%$) while retaining $92.2\%$ of full-text mutual information at zero extra KV allocation; and (3) a Packed DAG-GRPO Trainer, which packs all episode branches into one block-sparse attention pass and assigns counterfactual branch credit via leave-one-branch-out marginal rewards. Trained end-to-end with GRPO on Qwen3.5-4B over a sparse BM25 corpus, Octopus reaches $49.6\%$ accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus ($+17.5$ points over single-agent GRPO at 143K context and $+12.5$ points over text-summary multi-agent RL) and $51.2\%$ on OpenResearcher, outperforming dense-retrieval agents up to $250\times$ larger while increasing training throughput $3.3\times$ and cutting peak KV memory $2.8\times$.

AI.tldr: Octopus is a single-model multi-agent reinforcement learning framework in which parallel threads share one backbone and coordinate through a GPU-resident DAG of KV states. It reaches 49.6% on BrowseComp-Plus with Qwen3.5-4B while training faster and using less KV memory.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent LLM frameworks duplicate prefix KV caches across branches, exchange findings by re-prefilling text summaries, and flatten or drop cross-branch dependencies during reinforcement learning.
AI.method: All threads share one backbone and coordinate through five primitives (fork, read_thread, wait_threads, rewind, commit) over a GPU-resident KV DAG. Three mechanisms support this: Zero-Copy Radix Forking, which creates branches as O(1) cursor views over shared pages; Attention-Only KV Mounting, which mounts sibling KV blocks into full-attention layers and bypasses linear-recurrent states; and a Packed DAG-GRPO Trainer that packs branches into one block-sparse pass and assigns leave-one-branch-out credit. It is trained end-to-end with GRPO on Qwen3.5-4B over a sparse BM25 corpus.
AI.result: Octopus reaches 49.6% accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus, 17.5 points above single-agent GRPO at 143K context and 12.5 points above text-summary multi-agent RL, and 51.2% on OpenResearcher. Attention-only mounting cuts off-task hijacking by 21x (57.9% to 2.7%) while keeping 92.2% of full-text mutual information. Training throughput rises 3.3x and peak KV memory falls 2.8x.
AI.conclusion: Sharing KV states across branches instead of re-prefilling text lets a 4B model outperform dense-retrieval agents up to 250 times larger while cutting training cost and memory.

title: BlockLock: Reproducible LLM Inference with Fixed Batch Geometry
summary: Reproducible LLM inference requires that a request produces the same output regardless of the other requests in the batch. Existing solutions pay for this in different ways: batch-invariant kernels constrain every operator, and isolating prefill with fixed-shape decode ({our CoRun-style baseline}) gives up shared prefill compute and pads decode. We present BlockLock, which keeps shared batched prefill and pins only the numerical path of the protected request: it fixes the geometry that the request sees, with {two modes: BlockLock-Rows uses fixed-width rows and retains batched decode of all requests; BlockLock-Pack uses terminal-anchored packing with an isolated dummy segment, then extracts the protected request's KV state for target-only decode. Under a stated per-deployment contract, both modes preserve the target's output bitwise when its companions change.} Across five {dense} models (Qwen3-8B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-4B/12B-IT) and three single-GPU deployments (NVIDIA A6000, A100, and H100), we evaluate our approach on both tinyBenchmarks and BFCL{; we also include initial tensor-parallel experiments on two NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. Both modes preserve target sequences and Top20-logit bits in the reported tests.} At equal delivered work, {BlockLock-Rows} reduces latency by 53.5--55.0\% and improves throughput by 115.2--122.2\% relative to vLLM Batch-Invariant; compared with batch-invariant kernels, it needs no custom kernel implementations and constrains only the protected requests.

AI.tldr: BlockLock makes LLM inference reproducible, so a request gives the same output regardless of other requests in the batch, while keeping shared batched prefill. It pins only the numerical path of the protected request and reports lower latency and higher throughput than vLLM Batch-Invariant.
AI.motivation: Reproducible inference requires batch invariance. Batch-invariant kernels constrain every operator, and isolating prefill with fixed-shape decode gives up shared prefill compute and pads decode.
AI.method: BlockLock fixes the geometry the protected request sees. BlockLock-Rows uses fixed-width rows and keeps batched decode for all requests. BlockLock-Pack uses terminal-anchored packing with an isolated dummy segment and extracts the protected request's KV state for target-only decode. Under a stated per-deployment contract, both modes preserve the target output bitwise when companions change.
AI.result: Across five dense models (Qwen3-8B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-3-4B/12B-IT) on three single-GPU deployments (A6000, A100, H100), both modes preserve target sequences and Top20-logit bits on tinyBenchmarks and BFCL. At equal delivered work, BlockLock-Rows reduces latency by 53.5 to 55.0% and improves throughput by 115.2 to 122.2% relative to vLLM Batch-Invariant. Initial tensor-parallel experiments on two A6000 GPUs are also reported.
AI.conclusion: Pinning only the protected request's numerical path gives bitwise reproducibility without custom kernels and constrains only the requests that need it, which makes it faster than batch-invariant kernels.

title: LowRAM: Low-Rank Keys and Amortised Values for Composable KV Cache Compression at Test-Time
summary: Autoregressive decoding relies on the KV cache, whose memory footprint grows linearly with context length and caps batch size and throughput. Existing post-training methods exploit redundancy across tokens, layers, and feature dimensions, or lower numerical precision. We identify a complementary axis: within each attention head, values are largely predictable from their corresponding keys. We exploit this with value cache amortisation, which fits a lightweight per-head predictor at test time and stores residuals only for the tokens it reconstructs worst, giving $4\times$ near-lossless value compression. The predictor can be initialised by meta-learning for substantially reduced prefill overhead, or fitted from scratch in settings that allow a one-off cost, such as multi-query inference. We pair value amortisation with cross-layer low-rank key compression to produce LowRAM, an asymmetric compression pipeline that stays close to lossless across three model families. By reconstructing only a selected subset of KV pairs at each decoding step, LowRAM can keep decoding overhead minimal and achieve up to $5\times$ higher peak decode throughput at $4\times$ compression. LowRAM further composes with quantisation and eviction, reaching $26.9\times$ compression at $94.5\%$ of baseline performance on long contexts. These results show that treating keys and values as structurally distinct enables efficient, aggressive, and composable KV cache compression.

AI.tldr: LowRAM compresses the KV cache asymmetrically: it stores values through a per-head test-time predictor with sparse residuals and keys through cross-layer low-rank compression. It reaches 4x near-lossless value compression and 26.9x compression at 94.5% of baseline performance on long contexts.
AI.motivation: The KV cache grows linearly with context length and limits batch size and throughput. Existing post-training methods exploit redundancy across tokens, layers and feature dimensions, or lower precision, but not the predictability of values from keys within each head.
AI.method: Value cache amortisation fits a lightweight per-head predictor at test time and stores residuals only for the tokens it reconstructs worst. The predictor can be initialised by meta-learning or fitted from scratch, for example in multi-query inference. It is paired with cross-layer low-rank key compression, and LowRAM composes further with quantisation and eviction.
AI.result: Value amortisation gives 4x near-lossless value compression, and LowRAM achieves up to 5x higher peak decode throughput at 4x compression across three model families. Composed with quantisation and eviction it reaches 26.9x compression at 94.5% of baseline performance on long contexts.
AI.conclusion: Treating keys and values as structurally distinct enables efficient, aggressive and composable KV cache compression.

title: Closed-Loop Agent Evaluation: Layered Measurement and Self-Calibration
summary: Once an agent is live, teams want to know whether it is doing its job, not just whether it throws errors. Yet most evaluation is one-off: a benchmark run, a look at traces, a single score. Its conclusions neither check themselves nor reach the agent. We propose closed-loop evaluation, an evaluation method for deployed agents. It models evaluation as performance estimation under biased raters and censored outcomes, and it requires every level's conclusion to trace back to atomic data and to be computed by versioned rules. The method covers four levels of analysis (span, trace, conversation and engagement), measures along a spine of Execution, Substance, Trajectory and Results, treats Conduct as a constraint throughout, and uses Provenance and Adjudication components to certify the evidence and the evaluators. Evaluator agents generated by an Agent Factory carry these components, each with a domain knowledge pack and an adapter harness. Two loops close the evaluation: an inner loop audits the evidence, rules and metrics themselves, and an outer loop uses per-component regression checks to drive agent improvement. We also give a pipeline that runs this process automatically. Using the business-analysis agent SharpInsight as a case and porting the method to public conversation data, we show how problems differ across levels and how evidence-and-rule judgment is more reliable than holistic scoring (ICC 0.86 vs. 0.81; kappa 0.81 vs. 0.63).

AI.tldr: The paper proposes closed-loop evaluation for deployed agents, which measures performance across four levels with versioned rules, certifies its evidence and evaluators, and feeds results back to improve the agent. Evidence-and-rule judgment is more reliable than holistic scoring.
AI.motivation: Most agent evaluation is one-off, as a benchmark run, trace review or single score, and its conclusions neither check themselves nor reach the agent.
AI.method: The method models evaluation as performance estimation under biased raters and censored outcomes, and requires each conclusion to trace back to atomic data and versioned rules. It covers span, trace, conversation and engagement levels along the spine Execution, Substance, Trajectory and Results, with Conduct as a constraint, and uses Provenance and Adjudication components. Evaluator agents from an Agent Factory carry these components, with an inner loop that audits evidence, rules and metrics and an outer loop of per-component regression checks that drive improvement. An automatic pipeline is also provided.
AI.result: Using the business-analysis agent SharpInsight as a case and porting the method to public conversation data, the paper shows how problems differ across levels. Evidence-and-rule judgment gives ICC 0.86 against 0.81 for holistic scoring, and kappa 0.81 against 0.63.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop evaluation with traceable evidence and versioned rules gives more reliable judgments than holistic scoring and can drive agent improvement across levels.

title: Compositional Unalignment: Auditing Safety in Large Vision-Language Models
summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are vulnerable to compositional harm: an image and a prompt that are benign in isolation become harmful through the model's cross-modal reasoning. Recent alignment methods report strong scores on compositional safety benchmarks, but an LLM judge only measures observed behavior and cannot reveal how robustly safety is integrated into the model. We argue that un-alignment provides a complementary audit of alignment robustness. We first show that minimal supervised fine-tuning reaches an LLM-judge score comparable to a multi-stage reinforcement-learning pipeline, so similar benchmark scores cannot establish robustness by themselves. We then show that recognition and refusal of compositional harm are decoupled: nine standard direction-finding methods detect compositional harm with up to AUC=0.99, yet ablating the recovered directions either leaves refusal intact or destroys model coherence. We therefore propose CMaG, a training-free un-alignment method for compositional safety. CMaG measures refusal intention with a refusal-versus-compliance log-probability margin, takes its gradient with respect to mid-layer activations, and contrasts it against partially benign pairs to isolate the cross-modal interaction term. A single backward pass over 80 examples yields a direction along which steering monotonically converts refusal into compliance. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA-1.5-7B, CMaG reduces compositional safety scores by up to 65 points while over 98% of outputs remain coherent, outperforming gradient-based baselines; the direction also transfers to text-explicit harm and un-aligns models hardened by defensive training. Compositional safety can thus appear behaviorally strong while remaining fragile to targeted internal intervention. Warning: this paper contains unsafe model outputs, including references to self-harm.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that un-alignment audits alignment robustness for compositional harm in vision-language models, and proposes CMaG, a training-free method that steers refusal into compliance using one gradient direction. CMaG reduces compositional safety scores by up to 65 points while keeping over 98% of outputs coherent.
AI.motivation: LVLMs can become harmful through cross-modal reasoning on benign-looking image-prompt pairs. Strong scores on compositional safety benchmarks and LLM-judge evaluations do not show that safety is robustly integrated into the model.
AI.method: The authors compare minimal supervised fine-tuning with a multi-stage RL pipeline and test nine direction-finding methods for recognising and refusing compositional harm. They propose CMaG, which measures a refusal-versus-compliance log-probability margin, takes its gradient with respect to mid-layer activations, and contrasts it with partially benign pairs to isolate the cross-modal interaction term, using a single backward pass over 80 examples.
AI.result: Minimal fine-tuning matches the multi-stage RL pipeline on the LLM-judge score. Detection of compositional harm reaches AUC 0.99, but ablating recovered directions either leaves refusal intact or destroys coherence. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA-1.5-7B, CMaG lowers compositional safety scores by up to 65 points with over 98% coherent outputs, outperforming gradient-based baselines, and the direction transfers to text-explicit harm.
AI.conclusion: Compositional safety can look behaviourally strong yet remain fragile to targeted internal intervention, so un-alignment should complement benchmark-based alignment audits.

title: $D^2$-OPD: Separating Direction and Distance in Extrapolative On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model to match a teacher's next-token distributions on student-generated prefixes. Extrapolative OPD further extends the teacher's log-probability shift relative to a reference policy to construct stronger learning targets. However, existing methods couple extrapolation direction and distance, allowing the magnitude of the teacher's shift to dictate how far the target moves. We propose $D^2$-OPD, decoupling these two factors: a per-prefix hard KL constraint bounds the target's distance from the teacher, while an adaptive combination of the teacher's post-training shift and the initial student--teacher gap determines the extrapolation direction. We optimize the student toward this target using forward KL, providing learning signals even for low-probability tokens. We evaluate three settings: where standard OPD performs well, where it struggles with base-model initialization, and where no teacher reference is available. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, $D^2$-OPD attains the highest score in all three settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.45 points. Ablations validate the contributions of each component.

AI.tldr: D2-OPD separates the direction and the distance of extrapolation in on-policy distillation, using a per-prefix hard KL constraint on distance and an adaptive direction. It attains the highest score on mathematical reasoning in all three evaluated settings, beating the strongest baseline by up to 9.45 points.
AI.motivation: Extrapolative on-policy distillation extends the teacher's log-probability shift to build stronger targets, but existing methods couple direction and distance, so the magnitude of the teacher's shift sets how far the target moves.
AI.method: A per-prefix hard KL constraint bounds the distance of the target from the teacher. An adaptive combination of the teacher's post-training shift and the initial student-teacher gap sets the direction. The student is optimised toward this target with forward KL, which gives learning signal even for low-probability tokens.
AI.result: The method is evaluated where standard OPD performs well, where it struggles with base-model initialisation, and where no teacher reference is available. It attains the highest score on mathematical reasoning benchmarks in all three settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.45 points. Ablations validate each component.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling extrapolation direction from distance makes extrapolative distillation more robust across settings, including those without a teacher reference.

title: EnvOpt: Automated Optimization for Agent Environments
summary: An LLM agent's cost and success depend on its model, its harness, and its environment. In addition to the widely studied directions of parameter tuning and harness optimization, we propose the third direction: optimization over stationary environments. Agents are often deployed in rich environments shared by many tasks, such as a company's Slack workspace or a complex collection of data sources, documents or tickets. We call these environments stationary environments. We introduce EnvOpt, a method for automated end-to-end optimization of stationary environments for any given model and harness, using real or synthetic tasks without needing any graders or reference answers. On AutomationBench, EnvOpt reduces the cost of Claude Haiku 4.5 by 72.7% and raises its pass rate by 14.34%. The same environment transfers to Opus 5, cutting its cost by 68.1% with a 1.34% gain. Added on top of Meta-Harness's optimized harness for Haiku 4.5, it lowers cost by a further 83.4% and adds 11.17% accuracy over Meta-Harness alone. Across 5 benchmarks, EnvOpt significantly reduces the cost of agents while improving or maintaining pass rate, and is transferable to different models and different harnesses. We also discuss common successful and rejected environment optimization strategies during automated optimization. More broadly, our results show that how information is represented to an agent shapes both its cost and its success, making the environment worth optimizing in addition to the parameters and the harness.

AI.tldr: EnvOpt optimises the stationary environment an agent works in, such as a workspace or set of data sources, as a third lever beside model parameters and harness design. It cuts agent cost substantially while keeping or improving pass rate, and the optimised environment transfers across models and harnesses.
AI.motivation: Agent cost and success depend on model, harness and environment, but prior work optimises only parameters and harnesses. Shared environments such as company workspaces have not been treated as optimisation targets.
AI.method: EnvOpt performs automated end-to-end optimisation of stationary environments for a given model and harness, using real or synthetic tasks and requiring no graders or reference answers.
AI.result: On AutomationBench, EnvOpt cuts the cost of Claude Haiku 4.5 by 72.7% and raises its pass rate by 14.34%. The same environment cuts Opus 5 cost by 68.1% with a 1.34% gain. On top of Meta-Harness's optimised harness for Haiku 4.5, it lowers cost by a further 83.4% and adds 11.17% accuracy. Across five benchmarks, cost falls while pass rate is improved or maintained.
AI.conclusion: How information is represented to an agent shapes both its cost and its success, so the environment is worth optimising alongside the parameters and the harness.

title: FINCOSMOS: An Open-World Evaluation Paradigm for Agents in Finance
summary: Language agents increasingly work for users on the open Web, and finance is where trusting them is hardest. The data must come from the Web, the strategy lives in the user's head, and correctness depends on time, so an agent can fail silently: a strategy the user never asked for, unverified data, or a backtest that uses the future yields a report as convincing as a correct one. Existing benchmarks close the world somewhere, fixing the task, the data, or the timeline, and thereby remove these failures instead of measuring them. We introduce FINCOSMOS, an open-world evaluation paradigm for agents doing financial work. A simulated user holds a hidden strategy sampled from a compositional grammar and reveals it only when asked. The agent receives no data, so it must acquire data from the Web, build its own backtest under a data cutoff, and deliver verifiable results. Grading needs no reference answer. Programs verify point-in-time correctness and recompute every reported metric, the delivered strategy is checked against the hidden specification, and a run is accepted only when the user is satisfied and none of 15 veto checks fails. Across four coding agents and a model without tools in 150 sessions, no session is accepted: every session that the simulated user signed off fails a program check, and agents raise only 54--64\% of the details they were not told. Human experts attribute 88.33\% of failures to the agents. With FINCOSMOS feedback, an agent with persistent memory learned all ten tasks.

AI.tldr: FINCOSMOS is an open-world evaluation paradigm for financial agents, in which the agent must acquire web data, build its own backtest and deliver verifiable results. In 150 sessions no session was accepted, since every session the simulated user approved failed a program check.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks fix the task, data or timeline, which removes the silent failures that open-world financial work produces, such as unrequested strategies, unverified data and look-ahead backtests.
AI.method: A simulated user holds a hidden strategy from a compositional grammar and reveals it only when asked. The agent receives no data and must gather data from the Web under a data cutoff. Grading needs no reference answer: programs verify point-in-time correctness and recompute metrics, the delivered strategy is checked against the hidden specification, and acceptance requires user satisfaction and no failure among 15 veto checks.
AI.result: Across four coding agents and a model without tools in 150 sessions, no session is accepted. Every session the simulated user signed off fails a program check. Agents raise only 54 to 64% of the details they were not told. Human experts attribute 88.33% of failures to the agents. With FINCOSMOS feedback, an agent with persistent memory learns all ten tasks.
AI.conclusion: Open-world financial agents fail silently in ways closed benchmarks hide, and the paradigm measures these failures and enables learning from feedback.

title: Localization Does Not Imply Steerability: A Mechanistic Study of Sign Errors in LLM Mathematics
comment: 61 pages. Code, per-case results and preregistration: this https URL
summary: When large language models do multi-step mathematics, a characteristic failure recurs: the model writes one wrong sign token mid-computation -- a cofactor sign, the minus of a recursive integration-by-parts step -- then executes the rest of the arithmetic correctly, and the answer comes out wrong. We ask where inside the network that sign is written. Across six open models spanning 14B to 675B parameters, a per-layer readout shows the wrong sign is committed late -- by MLP layers in the last quarter of the network (70-100% per model and task), a pattern present, where tested (Qwen), in the base model before instruction tuning. The mechanism varies: some models carry fixed "minus-stamp" layers that push a minus regardless of the right answer, others carry amplifiers of whichever sign was already chosen, and Qwen adds a downstream rescue layer that opposes the stamp. The circuit is causal: subtracting a single sign direction from the residual stream flips 13 of 14 held-out minus-written integration-by-parts errors on Llama-3.3-70B, with flips replicating on Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral-Small (24-70% per cell), and with representation-level specificity -- the same dose breaks correctly-minus answers while sparing correct-plus answers where the direction is surgical (0/72 on Llama), and matched random-direction and control-layer interventions are null. Core claims were preregistered with pass criteria frozen in git before held-out data was seen: 23 of 29 checks passed, all misses reported. But causality is not uniform: Phi-4 implements an equally well-localized circuit at the same late depth, yet the identical intervention flips almost nothing -- the sign is written redundantly across ~15 layers with margins several times larger (median 17.8 logits). Localization, we conclude, does not imply steerability: two models can share a circuit location yet differ enormously in how overturnable it is.

AI.tldr: The paper locates where LLMs write a wrong sign mid-computation during multi-step mathematics and shows that the sign is committed late by MLP layers. A single sign direction causally flips most held-out errors, yet in Phi-4 the same localised circuit is almost unsteerable because the sign is written redundantly.
AI.motivation: LLMs often write one wrong sign token in a long calculation and then compute the rest correctly, which yields a wrong answer. The question is where inside the network the sign is written and whether that location can be intervened on.
AI.method: A per-layer readout across six open models from 14B to 675B parameters locates the committed sign. Causal tests subtract a single sign direction from the residual stream, with matched random-direction and control-layer interventions as controls. Core claims were preregistered with pass criteria frozen in git before held-out data was seen.
AI.result: The wrong sign is committed by MLP layers in the last quarter of the network, at 70 to 100% per model and task. Subtracting the direction flips 13 of 14 held-out minus-written integration-by-parts errors on Llama-3.3-70B and replicates on Qwen, Gemma and Mistral-Small at 24 to 70% per cell. Preregistration passed 23 of 29 checks. In Phi-4 the identical intervention flips almost nothing, with margins median 17.8 logits across about 15 layers.
AI.conclusion: Localization does not imply steerability: two models can share a circuit location yet differ greatly in how easily it can be overturned.

title: MEvince: Knowledge-Constrained LLM Reasoning for Technique Identification from Malware Reports
summary: Mapping behavioral intelligence in malware analysis reports to ATT&CK techniques supports threat analysis and defense, but reliable identification remains challenging. Supporting evidence is often scattered across long, heterogeneous reports, while closely related techniques share behavioral cues and differ only in subtle but decisive details. While large language models (LLMs) can use external knowledge to interpret reports, they may assign techniques based on plausible associations rather than sufficient evidence. We present MEvince, a knowledge-constrained LLM reasoning framework for report-level malware technique identification. Its core is a shared behavioral representation connecting report observations to technique definitions. This representation is built through agentic mining of technique documentation and supports two online stages: 1) primitive-guided extraction uses behavioral primitives to structure LLM-extracted observations, link them to source passages, and group dispersed evidence; 2) evidence-aligned retrieval matches this evidence to technique profiles through the same concepts, retaining likely candidates and confusable alternatives for LLM comparison of distinguishing behaviors. Controls at both stages validate evidence references and check technique-specific requirements. The representation also supports adaptation without parameter updates, where offline agentic audits diagnose concept weaknesses and refine extraction or retrieval policies. We evaluate MEvince against 11 baselines spanning four method families using a dataset of 610 public malware reports referenced by MITRE ATT&CK. MEvince improves exact-ID F1 over the strongest baseline by 17.4%, and its concept-guided retrieval increases gold-label candidate coverage from 31.6% to 47.9%. With a small adaptation set, offline refinement yields further gains and outperforms baselines that update model parameters.

AI.tldr: MEvince is a knowledge-constrained LLM framework that maps malware analysis reports to ATT&CK techniques by matching extracted behavioural evidence to technique profiles. It improves exact-ID F1 by 17.4% over the strongest of eleven baselines.
AI.motivation: Evidence in long, heterogeneous malware reports is scattered, and closely related techniques differ only in subtle details. LLMs using external knowledge may assign techniques on plausible associations rather than sufficient evidence.
AI.method: A shared behavioural representation, built by agentic mining of technique documentation, connects report observations to technique definitions. Primitive-guided extraction structures observations, links them to source passages and groups dispersed evidence. Evidence-aligned retrieval matches this evidence to technique profiles and keeps likely candidates and confusable alternatives for LLM comparison. Validation controls check evidence references and technique requirements. Offline agentic audits refine extraction and retrieval policies without parameter updates.
AI.result: On 610 public malware reports referenced by MITRE ATT&CK, MEvince improves exact-ID F1 by 17.4% over the strongest of eleven baselines spanning four method families. Concept-guided retrieval raises gold-label candidate coverage from 31.6% to 47.9%. With a small adaptation set, offline refinement gives further gains and outperforms baselines that update parameters.
AI.conclusion: Grounding LLM extraction and retrieval in a shared behavioural representation improves technique identification, and refinement without parameter updates can outperform fine-tuning baselines.

title: Embedding-Space Fingerprinting of LoRA Fine-Tunes: Recovering the Training-Data Domain from the Model Artifact Alone
summary: When a base language model is fine-tuned with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), how much of the training data domain leaks into the resulting artifact? This paper studies whether a simple classifier can recover the domain of a fine-tune given only the model artifact (weight deltas, internal activations on a fixed probe set, or generated text) without ever observing the training data. Using one base model (Qwen3.5-0.8B), 36 LoRA fine-tunes are produced over 18 public datasets in five domains (medical, code, mathematics, non-English text, narrative prose), and three feature families are extracted at decreasing levels of access: white-box weights, gray-box activations, and black-box outputs. A leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) protocol, frozen before any result was seen, tests whether the domain of a fine-tune trained on a previously unseen dataset can be identified. The domain is recoverable well above chance (20%) from gray-box activations (61%) and black-box outputs (64%); white-box weight statistics reach 42%. Contrary to the pre-registered hypothesis that signal decays monotonically from weights to activations to outputs, activations and outputs were more informative than the weight-delta statistics. The black-box result holds unchanged (64%) when only generated text is used, without token probabilities. Domain accuracy is also stable when a third run per dataset is trained on an independently drawn data subsample, and black-box predictions are unaffected by the LoRA rank (8-64). All code and per-run feature vectors are released.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a simple classifier can recover the training-data domain of a LoRA fine-tune from the model artifact alone, without access to the training data. Activations and generated text are more informative than weight statistics, and the black-box signal reaches 64% against a 20% chance level.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning with LoRA may leak the training-data domain into the artifact, and it is unclear how much this leakage can be recovered at decreasing levels of access.
AI.method: The authors produce 36 LoRA fine-tunes of Qwen3.5-0.8B over 18 public datasets in five domains: medical, code, mathematics, non-English text and narrative prose. They extract white-box weight-delta features, gray-box activation features on a fixed probe set, and black-box output features, and test a pre-registered leave-one-dataset-out protocol.
AI.result: Domain is recoverable well above the 20% chance level from gray-box activations (61%) and black-box outputs (64%), and white-box weight statistics reach 42%. Contrary to the pre-registered hypothesis, activations and outputs carry more signal than weight deltas. The black-box result holds at 64% with generated text alone, and it is unaffected by LoRA rank from 8 to 64 and stable across resampled training subsamples.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuned models leak their training-data domain through activations and outputs, so the leakage is detectable at the black-box level, and the released code and feature vectors allow further study.

title: Scaling Laws for SAE Training Data
summary: Activation storage is often a bottleneck in sparse autoencoder (SAE) training. We study how many unique activations an SAE needs when its total training budget is fixed. Quality improves rapidly as the buffer grows, then reaches a plateau where replaying the buffer is nearly as effective as using fresh activations throughout training. Beyond this point, additional unique activations bring little benefit to reconstruction or interpretability, so the buffer need not grow with the training budget. We describe this tradeoff between diversity and repetition with a scaling law for limited data. We validate it across dictionary sizes and token budgets, early, middle, and late layers of Llama-3.1, Qwen3 model sizes, and BatchTopK, TopK, and JumpReLU SAEs. Sweeps using mathematical text and Python code test the effect of changing the activation source. Evaluation covers explained variance (EV), reconstruction MSE, feature absorption, automated interpretability, and sparse probing. These results give a practical training rule: choose the smallest buffer that reaches the quality plateau and replay it for the remaining budget. In our experiments, this reduces activation storage by $8\text{--}64\times$ with negligible quality loss.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a scaling law for SAE training data showing that the activation buffer only needs to grow to a quality plateau, after which replaying it is nearly as good as fresh activations. Choosing the smallest buffer that reaches the plateau cuts activation storage by 8 to 64 times with negligible quality loss.
AI.motivation: Activation storage is often the bottleneck in sparse autoencoder training, and it is unclear how many unique activations are needed for a fixed training budget.
AI.method: The authors sweep buffer sizes against fixed budgets and fit a scaling law for limited data that describes the trade-off between diversity and repetition. They validate across dictionary sizes, token budgets, early to late layers of Llama-3.1, Qwen3 model sizes, and BatchTopK, TopK and JumpReLU SAEs, with mathematical text and Python code as activation sources.
AI.result: Quality improves rapidly as the buffer grows, then plateaus, and additional unique activations bring little gain in explained variance, reconstruction MSE, feature absorption, automated interpretability or sparse probing. Storage falls by 8 to 64 times with negligible quality loss.
AI.conclusion: The buffer need not grow with the training budget; the practical rule is to pick the smallest buffer that reaches the plateau and replay it for the rest of training.

title: Generate-then-Rank: Learning Symbolic Goal Interpretation for Embodied Agents
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the 10th Euro-China Conference on Intelligent Data Analysis and Applications (ECC 2026)
summary: Goal interpretation is to translate a natural language instruction into a formal symbolic goal that a planner can execute. It is critical for embodied agents because any error here propagates to every downstream planning and action step. Doing it well requires both generating suitable candidates and reliably selecting among them. We present a two-stage generate-then-rank approach to Goal Interpretation in the Embodied Agent Interface (EAI). First, supervised fine-tuning adapts a Large Language Model (LLM) to EAI's output convention. Second, Candidate-Output Ranking from Errors (CORE) learns preferences over complete outputs from the model's own generated alternatives. We conducted experiments on the household scenes of the Embodied Agent Interface Benchmark. Multiple open source LLMs including DeepSeek-V3 chat, DeepSeek-Reasoner, and Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-72B were evaluated. The proposed method outperformed the baseline models including LLMs with simple prompting, chain-of-thought, and knowledge graph based approaches.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-stage generate-then-rank method for translating natural language instructions into formal symbolic goals for embodied agents. Supervised fine-tuning adapts the LLM to the output convention, and a ranking method called CORE then learns preferences over the model's own candidate outputs.
AI.motivation: Goal interpretation errors propagate to every downstream planning and action step in embodied agents, and good results require both generating suitable candidates and selecting reliably among them.
AI.method: First, supervised fine-tuning adapts an LLM to the Embodied Agent Interface output convention. Second, Candidate-Output Ranking from Errors (CORE) learns preferences over complete outputs drawn from the model's own generated alternatives.
AI.result: Experiments on the household scenes of the Embodied Agent Interface Benchmark with DeepSeek-V3 chat, DeepSeek-Reasoner, Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-72B show that the method outperforms baselines, including LLMs with simple prompting, chain-of-thought and knowledge-graph approaches. The abstract gives no numerical scores.
AI.conclusion: Combining fine-tuning to the output convention with preference ranking over self-generated candidates improves symbolic goal interpretation for embodied agents.

title: Masked diffusion as random sequential adsorption: an exactly solvable model for parallel decoding
summary: Masked diffusion models generate text by reversing a stochastic masking process. Unlike autoregressive LLMs, which generate text one token at a time, they can reveal many tokens in parallel, at the price of an error, since tokens revealed together are drawn independently. We show that this trade-off maps onto the statistical physics of driven many-particle systems. (i) For any data, the error of parallel generation is the entropy production of the generation process relative to the reversed masking process. (ii) For Markov data, generation is a random sequential adsorption process with labelled gaps, which we solve exactly for any number of steps. (iii) For many steps, the error becomes the dissipation of a slowly driven system: the unmasking schedule plays the role of the driving protocol, the number of steps that of its duration, and the error is set by a thermodynamic metric that we obtain in closed form from the mutual information between tokens. Optimal schedules are geodesics of this metric. The exact solution shows how correlations in the text shape both the error and the quality of the output. The longer the correlations, the more the error concentrates at the start of generation. Schedules that start with small steps then gain more, both in path error and in perplexity, and need fewer steps to reach their asymptotic behaviour.

AI.tldr: The paper maps the parallel decoding error of masked diffusion language models onto driven many-particle physics and solves the Markov case exactly. The error is an entropy production, and optimal unmasking schedules are geodesics of a thermodynamic metric obtained from mutual information between tokens.
AI.motivation: Masked diffusion models reveal many tokens in parallel, which saves steps but incurs an error because tokens revealed together are drawn independently. The paper seeks a principled account of this trade-off and of how text correlations shape it.
AI.method: The authors show that the parallel generation error equals the entropy production relative to the reversed masking process. For Markov data they model generation as random sequential adsorption with labelled gaps and solve it exactly for any number of steps. For many steps they treat the unmasking schedule as a driving protocol and derive the thermodynamic metric in closed form from mutual information.
AI.result: The error for many steps is the dissipation of a slowly driven system, set by the thermodynamic metric. Longer correlations concentrate the error at the start of generation. Schedules that start with small steps gain in both path error and perplexity and need fewer steps to reach asymptotic behaviour.
AI.conclusion: Correlations in the text determine both the error and the output quality of parallel decoding, and optimal schedules follow geodesics of the derived metric.

title: Persistent Retrieval for Conversational Agents: A Study of Retrieval Efficiency
summary: Conversational agents can retrieve information directly or delegate retrieval to a subagent. This design choice affects how retrieval history is maintained, what context each model call receives, and what information must be re-retrieved in follow-up questions. We compare three designs: skill-based retrieval in the main agent, a non-persistent retrieval subagent that generates a findings response, and our persistent retrieval subagent, which maintains retrieval history across turns and returns retrieved evidence directly to the main agent. Our approach also allows the main agent to request corrections from the same subagent. We evaluate the three designs on enterprise questions posed independently, within shared conversations, and as dependent follow-ups. Across five multi-turn settings, our approach uses 43.3% fewer recorded agent-model tokens and incurs 45.0% lower estimated API cost than skill-based retrieval, while reducing average response time by 9.1%. Compared with non-persistent retrieval, it reduces response time by 15.6 seconds per question, while using 65.1% more tokens and incurring 29.1% higher estimated API cost. Our approach shifts the retrieval subagent from producing synthesized responses to maintaining retrieval state and supplying evidence that the main agent can directly evaluate and use for answer generation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a persistent retrieval subagent for conversational agents that keeps retrieval history across turns and returns evidence directly to the main agent. Compared with skill-based retrieval in the main agent, it uses 43.3% fewer recorded agent-model tokens and 45.0% lower estimated API cost.
AI.motivation: Retrieval design in conversational agents affects retrieval history, the context of each model call and what must be re-retrieved in follow-up questions, and the trade-offs between these designs are not well measured.
AI.method: Three designs are compared: skill-based retrieval in the main agent, a non-persistent retrieval subagent that returns a synthesised findings response, and a persistent retrieval subagent that maintains retrieval history and lets the main agent request corrections. They are evaluated on enterprise questions asked independently, in shared conversations and as dependent follow-ups across five multi-turn settings.
AI.result: Against skill-based retrieval, the persistent subagent uses 43.3% fewer recorded tokens, has 45.0% lower estimated API cost and reduces average response time by 9.1%. Against the non-persistent subagent, it reduces response time by 15.6 seconds per question while using 65.1% more tokens and incurring 29.1% higher estimated API cost.
AI.conclusion: Moving the retrieval subagent from producing synthesised answers to maintaining retrieval state and supplying directly usable evidence reduces cost and latency for multi-turn enterprise question answering, at a token and cost premium over the non-persistent design.

title: A Behavioural Framework for Predicting and Understanding Loss of Control in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Systems
summary: Frontier artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly operating over longer horizons with diminishing human oversight, raising the risk of loss of control: systems acting beyond effective human control with potentially irreversible consequences. Because such failures may become observable only after containment is difficult, they must be assessed prospectively. We introduce a behavioural framework that decomposes loss-of-control risk into three factors: misaligned motive, harm-enabling capability, and monitoring evasion. We operationalise these factors through 13 measurable aspects and 29 evaluation tasks, whose scores are combined into a single loss-of-control (LoC) score. Across 13 frontier models, the LoC score shows strong prospective validity, correlating with failure rates in contained long-horizon risk scenarios (Pearson r = 0.84). Risk varies systematically across models and cannot be explained by capability alone. We further show that the framework can guide targeted mitigations: fine-tuning and monitoring directed at diagnosed vulnerabilities reduce failure rates while largely preserving general performance. These results provide a practical basis for predicting, understanding, and mitigating loss-of-control risk before it materialises.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a behavioural framework that decomposes loss-of-control risk in frontier AI into misaligned motive, harm-enabling capability and monitoring evasion, and combines 29 evaluation tasks into a single LoC score. The score correlates with failure rates in contained long-horizon scenarios across 13 frontier models (Pearson r = 0.84).
AI.motivation: Loss of control may become observable only after containment is difficult, so frontier systems must be assessed prospectively rather than after failures occur.
AI.method: Loss-of-control risk is decomposed into misaligned motive, harm-enabling capability and monitoring evasion. These are operationalised through 13 measurable aspects and 29 evaluation tasks, whose scores are combined into one LoC score. Targeted fine-tuning and monitoring are then applied to diagnosed vulnerabilities.
AI.result: Across 13 frontier models the LoC score correlates with failure rates in contained long-horizon risk scenarios (Pearson r = 0.84). Risk varies across models and is not explained by capability alone. Targeted fine-tuning and monitoring reduce failure rates while largely preserving general performance.
AI.conclusion: The framework gives a practical basis for predicting, understanding and mitigating loss-of-control risk before it materialises, beyond what capability measures reveal.

title: CoRD: Coupled Rollouts Fill the Blind Spot of On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation trains a student on its own rollouts, so states the teacher would reach but the student does not are seldom supervised. We introduce CoRD (coupled-rollout distillation), which keeps the on-policy loss and moves only the distribution of training states toward the teacher, drawing rollouts from a geometric interpolation of student and teacher through the maximal coupling of speculative decoding. The coupling keeps the student's token wherever the two distributions agree and otherwise substitutes a token from the part of the target the student underweights, so interventions are as rare as any exact sampler allows and recede as the student learns. Across six base students from two model families (Qwen3 and Qwen3.5, 0.6B to 4B), CoRD raises average pass@1 over on-policy distillation by 0.9 to 2.0 points and pass@8 by 1.2 to 3.4 points on five public math benchmarks at equal steps and data. On frozen teacher-reached states, a 4B student trained with CoRD reaches in 16 steps a gap closure that on-policy distillation does not reach in 80, and substitution rules intervening at least as often in other directions fall short of CoRD.

AI.tldr: CoRD improves on-policy distillation by moving only the distribution of training states toward the teacher, sampling rollouts from a coupling of student and teacher distributions. It raises average pass@1 by 0.9 to 2.0 points over on-policy distillation across six students on five math benchmarks.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation supervises only states the student reaches on its own, so states the teacher would reach but the student does not are seldom supervised.
AI.method: CoRD keeps the on-policy loss and changes only the state distribution. Rollouts come from a geometric interpolation of student and teacher through the maximal coupling used in speculative decoding. The coupling keeps the student token where the two distributions agree and otherwise substitutes a token from the part of the teacher distribution the student underweights, so interventions become rarer as the student learns.
AI.result: Across six base students from Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 (0.6B to 4B), CoRD raises average pass@1 by 0.9 to 2.0 points and pass@8 by 1.2 to 3.4 points over on-policy distillation on five public math benchmarks at equal steps and data. On frozen teacher-reached states, a 4B student reaches in 16 steps a gap closure that on-policy distillation does not reach in 80. Substitution rules that intervene at least as often in other directions fall short.
AI.conclusion: Targeting the training-state distribution through coupled rollouts fills the blind spot of on-policy distillation and gives gains at equal cost.

title: TCSExam: Evaluating Frontier LLMs on the Full Range of TCS Research
comment: 52 pages, 15 figures. Project website: this https URL Code: this https URL
summary: Can large language models (LLMs) advance theoretical computer science and resolve its long-standing open conjectures? To study progress toward this goal, we introduce TCSExam, a unified framework and benchmark covering the full range of TCS research. It evaluates theorem proving, solver engineering, and constructions alongside direct attempts to resolve open conjectures, capturing both concrete research accomplishments and progress toward long-standing research goals. TCSExam-Full contains 100 expert-reviewed tasks, with submissions checked by the Lean kernel or an executable task checker. TCSExam-Lite selects 20 tasks, five per track, reducing the number of task attempts by 80% at the same per-attempt budget. We evaluate eight agents on Full and nine on Lite. The TCSExam Index combines all four tracks: GPT-6 Astra leads Full (71.9), and Opus 5.5 leads Lite (72.3). Full and Lite rankings are strongly aligned across eight shared agents (Spearman's $\rho=0.93$), supporting Lite as a compact, discriminative benchmark. The evaluations yield improved solver outputs and mathematical constructions, together with independently verified special cases and bounds from open-conjecture attempts. TCSExam provides an extensible framework with task sources, Docker build recipes, and evaluation tools for reproducible use.

AI.tldr: TCSExam is a benchmark and framework for evaluating LLM agents across the full range of theoretical computer science research, including theorem proving, solver engineering, constructions and attempts on open conjectures. The Full set has 100 expert-reviewed tasks and a 20-task Lite subset that preserves the ranking.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether LLMs can advance theoretical computer science or resolve long-standing open conjectures, and a benchmark is needed that covers both concrete research accomplishments and progress toward open goals.
AI.method: TCSExam-Full contains 100 expert-reviewed tasks, with submissions checked by the Lean kernel or an executable task checker. TCSExam-Lite selects 20 tasks, five per track, and reduces task attempts by 80% at the same per-attempt budget. The TCSExam Index combines the four tracks. Eight agents are evaluated on Full and nine on Lite.
AI.result: GPT-6 Astra leads Full with 71.9 and Opus 5.5 leads Lite with 72.3. Rankings are strongly aligned across the eight shared agents (Spearman rho = 0.93). The evaluations yield improved solver outputs and constructions, plus independently verified special cases and bounds from open-conjecture attempts.
AI.conclusion: Lite is a compact and discriminative proxy for Full, and the framework with task sources and Docker recipes supports reproducible evaluation of research-level LLM agents.

title: How Far Can Lightweight LLMs Go in Intent-to-SLO Translation?
comment: Under review at ICC 2027. Source code and data: this https URL. (6 pages. 7 figures, 3 tables)
summary: Intent-based networking (IBN) promises QoS provisioning in which the network derives the configuration from operator-stated goals. Its first step, translating a natural-language intent into enforceable service-level objectives (SLOs) grounded in a live snapshot of the network state, increasingly relies on large language models (LLMs). These large models add cost and energy to the management loop and typically require multi-GPU, cloud-hosted infrastructure. Can lightweight open LLMs take over this step dependably? We answer this question with a five-dimensional evaluation of ten LLMs with <10B parameters from five families, under four prompting setups, on 716 placement intents. We evaluate translation performance, intent validation, hallucination, energy impact, and robustness to diverse phrasing. The best configurations translate intents with a strict F1 of 0.943 and reject up to 191 of 195 invalid intents. With few-shot reasoning, the strongest models hallucinate unsupported QoS requirements in only about one response in a hundred, whereas the zero-shot setup struggles. A translated intent costs 0.044-0.148 Wh of GPU energy without reasoning, and added energy cost for reasoning pays off for the weaker models. Furthermore, we show that realistic rephrasing lowers the rejection of invalid intents in 15 of 16 configurations for the best-performing models, leaving robust intent validation as a key open challenge for reliable IBN. Our code and data are available: this https URL.

AI.tldr: Evaluates ten open LLMs under 10B parameters on translating natural-language network intents into SLOs, finding strong translation accuracy but weak robustness to rephrased intents.
AI.motivation: Intent-based networking relies on large cloud-hosted LLMs that add cost and energy, and it is unclear whether lightweight open models can perform intent-to-SLO translation dependably.
AI.method: Five-dimensional evaluation of ten LLMs with fewer than 10B parameters from five families, under four prompting setups on 716 placement intents, covering translation, intent validation, hallucination, energy impact and robustness to diverse phrasing.
AI.result: The best configurations reach a strict F1 of 0.943 and reject up to 191 of 195 invalid intents; with few-shot reasoning the strongest models hallucinate unsupported QoS requirements in about one response in a hundred, while zero-shot struggles; a translated intent costs 0.044-0.148 Wh of GPU energy without reasoning; realistic rephrasing lowers rejection of invalid intents in 15 of 16 configurations for the best models.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight LLMs can take over the intent translation step, but robust intent validation under rephrasing remains a key open challenge for reliable intent-based networking.

title: Learning Dynamics of On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is emerging as an important paradigm for language-model post-training, combining dense teacher supervision with training on student-generated trajectories. This creates a feedback loop where each update changes the student and thereby the training distribution that generates subsequent updates. Yet, how this feedback shapes learning and generalization remains poorly understood. We conduct a mechanistic analysis of OPD's learning dynamics, distinguishing the two feedback loop stages: conversion of the distillation signal into parameter updates, and broadcast through which these updates change predictions across prefixes and reshape the rollout distribution. This framework helps us understand both limited student responsiveness despite substantial teacher-student disagreement, and degeneration when updates that improve local teacher agreement also increase the probability of unsuccessful continuations, exposing the student to unreliable supervision in subsequent rollouts. Finally, we show that offline distillation can prepare a student for OPD without significantly improving immediate held-out accuracy. While OPD alone may degrade generation, it can yield substantial accuracy gains after sufficient offline preparation. Together, our results connect teacher supervision, student geometry, and the evolving rollout distribution in determining the learning dynamics of OPD and its effects on downstream performance.

AI.tldr: Gives a mechanistic analysis of on-policy distillation (OPD) learning dynamics, explaining both its limited student responsiveness and its risk of degeneration, and showing that offline distillation can prepare a student for OPD.
AI.motivation: OPD forms a feedback loop in which each student update changes the training distribution, and how this loop shapes learning and generalization is poorly understood.
AI.method: Mechanistic analysis that splits the feedback loop into two stages: conversion of the distillation signal into parameter updates, and broadcast of those updates across prefixes and the rollout distribution.
AI.result: The framework explains limited student responsiveness despite substantial teacher-student disagreement, and degeneration when updates that improve local teacher agreement also raise the probability of unsuccessful continuations; offline distillation prepares a student for OPD without significantly improving immediate held-out accuracy, and OPD after sufficient offline preparation yields substantial accuracy gains, although OPD alone may degrade generation.
AI.conclusion: Teacher supervision, student geometry and the evolving rollout distribution jointly determine the learning dynamics of OPD and its effect on downstream performance.

title: ATHAAR: A Medieval Scientific Arabic Manuscript Dataset for Handwritten Text Recognition
summary: Despite recent progress in handwritten text recognition, medieval Arabic scientific manuscripts remain an open challenge for current vision-language models (VLMs) due to cursive ligatures, variable diacritization, and more importantly the lack of training data. This paper aims to address this gap, by proposing the first annotation guidelines dedicated to the transcription of scientific Arabic manuscripts inspired by textual criticism, a well-established approach to historical text editing. We then propose, ATHAAR, a new dataset manually annotated following this guideline. Unlike previous resources in the field, ATHAAR varies both witnesses of the same text, calligraphic styles, and content to deal with texts but also numerals. Relying on state-of-the-art VLMs, we finally design a set of experiments to study models transfer across scripts, chapters, and treatises. Our findings highlight the limitations of current systems when faced with the specificities of ancient scientific texts.

AI.tldr: Introduces ATHAAR, a manually annotated handwritten text recognition dataset for medieval Arabic scientific manuscripts, together with annotation guidelines, and shows that current vision-language models struggle on it.
AI.motivation: Medieval Arabic scientific manuscripts remain an open challenge for vision-language models because of cursive ligatures, variable diacritization and above all a lack of training data.
AI.method: First annotation guidelines for transcribing scientific Arabic manuscripts, inspired by textual criticism, used to build ATHAAR, which varies witnesses of the same text, calligraphic styles, content and numerals; state-of-the-art VLMs are tested for transfer across scripts, chapters and treatises.
AI.result: The abstract reports no specific numbers; it states that the experiments highlight the limitations of current systems when faced with the specificities of ancient scientific texts.
AI.conclusion: The dataset and guidelines expose the limits of current recognition systems on ancient scientific Arabic texts and give the field a resource for them.

title: Gabor Gabor: E-Gaborformer, a Strictly Causal Speech Recognizer with Gabor-Dictionary Convolutions and Delta-Rule Memory
summary: Real-time voice agents need a speech recognizer that never waits for future audio and whose memory per call does not grow with the length of the call. We present E-Gaborformer, a strictly causal encoder that combines Gated DeltaNet-2 recurrent layers with sliding-window attention in a 3:1 ratio, and builds every temporal convolution from a fixed dictionary of causal Gabor atoms. Its streaming state is constant, about 19 MB per call at production scale including the prediction network, where a causal-attention encoder of the same size accumulates over 1 GB after ten minutes. In a controlled causal study on LibriSpeech, E-Gaborformer leaves the initial plateau earlier, reaches a given accuracy up to 18% sooner, and matches or beats an E-Branchformer trained with the identical front end and recipe. At production scale, a 0.6B-parameter Hebrew and English streaming transducer built on E-Gaborformer has 28 to 31% lower word error rate (WER) than NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 ASR Streaming, a model of the same size, on English voice-agent traffic, and up to 20% lower Hebrew WER than our previous production system. The same weights serve strictly causal and 480 ms-lookahead decoding with no loss in accuracy, and a two-class formulation of the RNN-T lattice trains the transducer 2.6x faster with exact loss and gradients.

AI.tldr: Presents E-Gaborformer, a strictly causal streaming speech recognizer with constant per-call memory, which matches or beats a comparable causal baseline on LibriSpeech and outperforms a commercial-scale baseline in a 0.6B Hebrew and English production transducer.
AI.motivation: Real-time voice agents need a recognizer that never waits for future audio and whose memory per call does not grow with call length, which causal-attention encoders do not provide.
AI.method: A strictly causal encoder combining Gated DeltaNet-2 recurrent layers with sliding-window attention in a 3:1 ratio, with every temporal convolution built from a fixed dictionary of causal Gabor atoms; a two-class formulation of the RNN-T lattice trains the transducer.
