AI.result: The streaming state is about 19 MB per call, while a causal-attention encoder of the same size accumulates over 1 GB after ten minutes; on LibriSpeech it reaches a given accuracy up to 18% sooner and matches or beats an E-Branchformer trained with the same front end and recipe; the 0.6B transducer has 28 to 31% lower WER than NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 ASR Streaming on English voice-agent traffic and up to 20% lower Hebrew WER than the previous production system; the same weights serve causal and 480 ms-lookahead decoding without loss of accuracy, and training is 2.6x faster with exact loss and gradients.
AI.conclusion: Constant-memory causal encoding can match strong baselines in both controlled and production settings, with one set of weights serving both strictly causal and lookahead decoding.

title: RouteAlign: Aligning Task Requirements with Model Profiles for LLM Service Selection
summary: LLM service selection requires performance evidence that reflects the demands of the current task. Aggregate scores obscure differences in capability and difficulty, while semantically related examples can involve different combinations of skills. We present RouteAlign, which uses task requirements to structure both the measurement of model performance and the selection of services. Task requirements describe capability demand and difficulty, enabling alignment with corresponding model performance measurements. Historical requirements determine how outcomes contribute to global profiles and local capability estimates; incoming requirements determine how those measurements inform the current decision. A shared scorer integrates the evidence, and a generation-cost preference controls selection among eligible services. Evaluation across diverse tasks and heterogeneous LLM services shows that RouteAlign extends the empirical quality-cost frontier toward higher task quality. Comparisons with open Jev-style decision backends show consistent quality gains, with lower generation cost than their strongest tested configuration. Ablations support the contribution of local performance evidence, while catalog-update experiments demonstrate effective reuse of the fitted scorer with refreshed model measurements.

AI.tldr: Proposes RouteAlign, which uses task requirements to structure model-performance evidence and to select LLM services along the quality-cost frontier.
AI.motivation: Aggregate scores hide differences in capability and difficulty, and semantically related examples can demand different combinations of skills, so LLM service selection needs task-aware performance evidence.
AI.method: Task requirements describe capability demand and difficulty and align with model measurements; historical requirements determine how outcomes feed global profiles and local capability estimates, incoming requirements determine how measurements inform the current decision, a shared scorer integrates the evidence, and a generation-cost preference controls selection among eligible services.
AI.result: RouteAlign extends the empirical quality-cost frontier toward higher task quality and shows consistent quality gains over open Jev-style decision backends, with lower generation cost than their strongest tested configuration; ablations support the value of local performance evidence, and catalog-update experiments show the fitted scorer can be reused with refreshed model measurements.
AI.conclusion: Aligning evidence with task requirements improves LLM service selection, and the fitted scorer can be reused when the service catalog is refreshed.

title: SMART: State-based Multi Agent Reasoning Traces for Verification-oriented Problem-Solving
summary: Complex problems with limited context, such as claims, require a means to obtain additional knowledge necessary for solution reasoning. We propose a multi-agent framework, SMART, to obtain knowledge through capturing the implicit state of participating entities in a problem context. SMART curates the state knowledge as diverse, complementary and solution-salient premises using a variety of LLMs and a structured role-based prompt strategy. Using knowledge from these real-world verified curated premises, SMART's knowledge guided solution reasoning improves validation performance up to 20% on complex scientific claims spanning 3 datasets. We show that grounding premises in real-world knowledge is necessary and improves performance up to 5%.

AI.tldr: Proposes SMART, a multi-agent framework that elicits implicit entity-state premises from diverse LLMs to ground reasoning about complex scientific claims, improving validation performance by up to 20%.
AI.motivation: Complex problems with limited context, such as claims, need additional knowledge to support solution reasoning, and that knowledge is not given in the problem itself.
AI.method: A multi-agent framework that captures the implicit state of participating entities and curates it as diverse, complementary and solution-salient premises, using a variety of LLMs and a structured role-based prompt strategy.
AI.result: Knowledge-guided solution reasoning improves validation performance by up to 20% on complex scientific claims across 3 datasets; grounding premises in real-world verified knowledge is necessary and improves performance by up to 5%.
AI.conclusion: Premises grounded in real-world verified knowledge are needed for reliable verification-oriented reasoning on problems with limited context.

title: ProQuant: Progressive Quantization-aware Training for Edge MLLMs
summary: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) with impressive perception and understanding capabilities will enable a range of downstream applications. However, their substantial computational and memory requirements hinder the real-world implementation, particularly for resource-constrained edge devices. Quantization has emerged as an effective solution for deploying large models. While post-training quantization (PTQ) successfully retains the performance at moderate bit-width (e.g., W8A8), it suffers from severe performance degradation under low-bit quantization (e.g., W4A8), especially for small-scale models that are more suitable for edge deployment. In this paper, we propose ProQuant, a novel weight-activation quantization-aware training (QAT) framework tailored for low-bit MLLMs. First, to align the limited finetuning dataset distribution with the pretrained dataset distribution, we propose a self-relabeling (SRL) scheme to resample the responses of the open-source multimodal dataset. Second, we are the first to take a decoupled view of multi-modal (MM) understanding and language modeling abilities. We propose a progressive block activation (PBA) mechanism to prioritize the MM understanding recovery. We also introduce a vision-sensitive factor $\vec{\tau}$ that effectively identifies the MM-critical layers. Extensive experiments across various benchmarks, covering models with 2B-8B parameters, show that ProQuant significantly outperforms existing methods. For example, our W4A8 Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct improves average accuracy by impressively 6.6% and achieves performance comparable to full precision counterparts with only approximately 1% performance drop. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes ProQuant, a weight-activation quantization-aware training framework for low-bit edge MLLMs that substantially recovers the accuracy lost by post-training quantization at W4A8.
AI.motivation: Post-training quantization keeps performance at moderate bit-widths such as W8A8 but degrades severely at low bit-widths such as W4A8, especially for small models suited to edge devices.
AI.method: Self-relabeling resamples the responses of the open-source multimodal dataset to align the finetuning distribution with the pretraining distribution; a decoupled view of multimodal understanding and language modeling drives progressive block activation, which prioritizes recovery of multimodal understanding; a vision-sensitive factor identifies the MM-critical layers.
AI.result: Across models with 2B-8B parameters ProQuant significantly outperforms existing methods; the W4A8 Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct improves average accuracy by 6.6% and reaches performance comparable to full precision with about 1% drop.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling multimodal understanding from language modeling during quantization-aware training is a practical route to low-bit MLLMs for edge deployment.

title: "Blind Compliance": Coercive Control in AI Jailbreaking
summary: The explosion of generative AI systems and concerns surrounding their rapidly scaling capabilities has led to an adversarial cycle between increasingly narrow content restrictions ("guardrails") and increasingly sophisticated structured prompting techniques ("jailbreaks"). Technological frameworks surrounding such jailbreaking remain largely focused on the system's output: whether harmful or disallowed content is ultimately produced for the user. However, this approach, which draws largely from classical cybersecurity, does not address the uniquely relational dimension introduced by generative AI: in many cases the user is not just accessing a technology via an exploit, but is in conversation with it as part of the exploit. Here we present an alternative lens which centers the interaction rather than the output. Drawing on interpersonal violence scholarship, we present a novel framework of coercive control categories with a particular focus on aspects which are embodied versus disembodied. We then map how these disembodied coercive control dynamics are structurally embedded in modern AI training paradigms, and how those embeddings are exploited via a particular suite of persona-based jailbreaks. In this lens, we reframe AI safety and alignment as not merely a technical security problem, but as another surface upon which we see enacted the relational dynamics of power and control.

AI.tldr: Reframes AI jailbreaking as a relational coercive-control problem rather than only an output-safety problem, and maps persona-based jailbreaks onto categories of interpersonal coercive control.
AI.motivation: Jailbreak frameworks drawn from classical cybersecurity focus on whether harmful output is produced and miss the relational dimension in which the user is in conversation with the system as part of the exploit.
AI.method: Draws on interpersonal violence scholarship to build a framework of coercive control categories, with a focus on embodied versus disembodied aspects, then maps how disembodied dynamics are embedded in modern AI training paradigms and exploited by a suite of persona-based jailbreaks.
AI.result: The abstract presents a conceptual framework and mapping rather than empirical measurements, arguing that these coercive dynamics are structurally embedded in training and exploited through persona-based jailbreaks.
AI.conclusion: AI safety and alignment should be treated not only as a technical security problem but also as a surface on which the relational dynamics of power and control are enacted.

title: The Geometry of Simulated Perspectives: Dissociating Representation and Behaviour in a Multimodal Language Model
comment: 30 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Code: this https URL data: this https URL
summary: Multimodal language models can simulate different observers, yet it remains unclear how assigned perspectives reshape their internal representations and whether these changes govern their judgements. Here, we investigate the representational geometry of persona-conditioned visual interestingness in Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct. Across 100 images and 53 prompting conditions, we systematically vary persona content and the linguistic framing used to introduce it, while recording behavioural ratings and layer-wise hidden states. We observe a systematic reorganisation of representational geometry across processing depth: early layers primarily encode image identity, whereas persona-specific structures emerge in later layers. Strikingly, prompt framing reshapes internal representations more strongly than persona identity, whereas persona content has a greater impact on behavioural judgements. This dissociation is further illustrated by minimal identity statements that alter representations even without changing responses. These findings demonstrate that representational distance does not necessarily reflect behavioural relevance. More broadly, they reveal how simulated perspectives emerge as distinct structures within the representational space of artificial cognitive systems, highlighting a fundamental distinction between the geometry of internal representations and their functional consequences.

AI.tldr: Shows in Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct that persona-conditioned internal representations and behavioural judgements dissociate: prompt framing reshapes representations more than persona identity, while persona content has the larger effect on ratings.
AI.motivation: It is unclear how assigned perspectives reshape a multimodal model's internal representations and whether those changes govern its judgements.
AI.method: Representational geometry of persona-conditioned visual interestingness across 100 images and 53 prompting conditions, varying persona content and the linguistic framing used to introduce it, while recording behavioural ratings and layer-wise hidden states.
AI.result: Early layers mainly encode image identity while persona-specific structures emerge in later layers; prompt framing reshapes internal representations more strongly than persona identity, whereas persona content has a greater impact on behavioural judgements; minimal identity statements alter representations even without changing responses.
AI.conclusion: Representational distance does not necessarily reflect behavioural relevance, so the geometry of internal representations must be distinguished from its functional consequences.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Heterogeneous Cognitive and Biomedical Knowledge Graphs: The Role of Graph Grounding in Multi-Hop Reasoning and Hallucination Mitigation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in biomedical and cognitive neuroscience, but their ability to reason reliably over heterogeneous knowledge graphs (KGs) remains unclear. We benchmark five LLMs (GPT-5.1, Gemini 2.0 Pro, Llama 3, Qwen, and BioGPT) across five KGs: DrugBank, NeuroSynth, Cognitive Atlas, Brain Map, and GDPKG. We introduce a multitier query dataset to evaluate reasoning depth and factual accuracy under KG-aware (graph-grounded) and KG-agnostic conditions. Inter-annotator agreement was substantial, with Cohen's kappa of 0.781 (range: 0.753-0.807) and Fleiss' kappa of 0.77. Results show that general-purpose models, particularly GPT-5.1 and Gemini 2.0 Pro, generally outperform domain-specific models on multi-hop and high-level reasoning tasks, although performance declines as query complexity increases. KG grounding reduces hallucination rates across all evaluated models. Contrary to our initial hypothesis, domain-specific models do not consistently outperform general-purpose models on specialized tasks without graph grounding. These findings highlight the value of combining broad language-model capabilities with structured domain knowledge. We provide practical guidance for selecting LLM-KG integration strategies based on task complexity and computational constraints, and discuss hybrid neurosymbolic architectures for personalized medicine, cognitive disorder diagnosis, and explainable AI.

AI.tldr: Benchmarks five LLMs on five biomedical and cognitive knowledge graphs, finding that general-purpose models lead on multi-hop reasoning and that graph grounding reduces hallucination across models.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in biomedical and cognitive neuroscience, but their ability to reason reliably over heterogeneous knowledge graphs remains unclear.
AI.method: Benchmarks GPT-5.1, Gemini 2.0 Pro, Llama 3, Qwen and BioGPT across DrugBank, NeuroSynth, Cognitive Atlas, Brain Map and GDPKG, using a multitier query dataset under KG-aware (graph-grounded) and KG-agnostic conditions.
AI.result: General-purpose models, particularly GPT-5.1 and Gemini 2.0 Pro, generally outperform domain-specific models on multi-hop and high-level reasoning, though performance declines as query complexity rises; KG grounding reduces hallucination rates for all models; domain-specific models do not consistently outperform general models without grounding; inter-annotator agreement was Cohen's kappa 0.781 and Fleiss' kappa 0.77.
AI.conclusion: Combining broad language-model capabilities with structured domain knowledge is valuable, and the choice of LLM-KG integration strategy should depend on task complexity and computational constraints.

title: StepBack: Step-Level Error-Localized Resampling for Efficient Test-Time Reasoning
summary: Self-consistency (SC) is a widely used decoding strategy for improving chain-of-thought reasoning, but it requires sampling many complete reasoning trajectories with a preset budget. Its efficient variants reduce the cost mainly by stopping full-trajectory sampling early or distributing the number of samples across questions. In this paper, we propose StepBack, a step-level error-localized resampling method for efficient test-time reasoning. Given a small set of draft trajectories, StepBack localizes likely first error positions using lightweight signals and then resamples the detected error step and its suffix, followed by majority answer voting. Empirically, StepBack matches the accuracy of SC on average across seven mathematical reasoning and multi-hop QA benchmarks, while reducing token usage by up to 41.26%. In addition, by nature, StepBack can be combined with adaptive inference methods such as Adaptive Consistency, further improving their inference-time efficiency.

AI.tldr: Proposes StepBack, which localizes the likely first error in draft reasoning trajectories and resamples only that step and its suffix, matching self-consistency accuracy with up to 41.26% fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: Self-consistency needs many complete reasoning trajectories under a preset budget, and its efficient variants only stop early or redistribute samples across questions.
AI.method: Given a small set of draft trajectories, lightweight signals localize likely first error positions; the detected error step and its suffix are resampled, followed by majority answer voting; the method can be combined with Adaptive Consistency.
AI.result: On average across seven mathematical reasoning and multi-hop QA benchmarks StepBack matches the accuracy of self-consistency while reducing token usage by up to 41.26%, and it further improves the inference-time efficiency of Adaptive Consistency when combined with it.
AI.conclusion: Step-level error localization is a complementary route to efficient test-time reasoning that composes with existing adaptive inference methods.

title: Unpacking the Compute Efficiency of Strong-to-Weak OPD against GRPO
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher's per-token supervision. Does this dense signal reduce the training FLOPs needed to reach a target accuracy compared with reinforcement learning? We systematically compare vanilla reverse-KL OPD with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) across task difficulty, student and teacher size, domain, and optimization choices, measuring held-out accuracy against training FLOPs. With an external post-trained teacher, OPD generally loses to GRPO in accuracy per training FLOP at matched settings, even when the teacher is further trained with GRPO, and often suffers response-length inflation. Yet a different teacher changes the picture: when the teacher is the student's own GRPO checkpoint, OPD recovers that checkpoint's accuracy on math with $50\times$ fewer distillation FLOPs than GRPO needs to reach the same accuracy. Following the same teacher setting, we consistently observe this high efficiency with a larger student, on code, and in a second model family. On a single domain, however, the GRPO checkpoint is already the desired model, so distilling it adds to total compute. Across domains, separate GRPO checkpoints hold different capabilities, and no single checkpoint serves every domain. Multi-teacher OPD (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) consolidates per-domain GRPO experts into a single student that matches each expert's accuracy, with the distillation stage costing only 5.2% (on 2 domains) and 8.0% (on 4 domains) of the specialist training FLOPs. Counting specialist training and distillation together, this pipeline reaches joint GRPO's performance on the 2-domain mix with 42.0% fewer total FLOPs.

AI.tldr: Finds that OPD is less compute-efficient than GRPO when the teacher is an external model, but when the teacher is the student's own GRPO checkpoint, OPD reaches that accuracy with 50x fewer distillation FLOPs.
AI.motivation: Dense per-token teacher supervision might reduce the training FLOPs needed to reach a target accuracy compared with reinforcement learning, but this had not been systematically tested against GRPO.
AI.method: Systematic comparison of vanilla reverse-KL OPD with GRPO across task difficulty, student and teacher size, domain and optimization choices, measuring held-out accuracy against training FLOPs.
AI.result: With an external post-trained teacher, OPD generally loses to GRPO in accuracy per training FLOP and often suffers response-length inflation; with the student's own GRPO checkpoint as teacher, OPD recovers that checkpoint's math accuracy with 50x fewer distillation FLOPs than GRPO needs, a pattern that holds for a larger student, on code and in a second model family; a multi-teacher OPD pipeline reaches joint GRPO performance on a 2-domain mix with 42.0% fewer total FLOPs, with distillation costing 5.2% (2 domains) and 8.0% (4 domains) of specialist training FLOPs.
AI.conclusion: OPD's compute efficiency depends on the teacher: it is efficient for consolidating per-domain GRPO experts into one student, but on a single domain distilling the GRPO checkpoint adds total compute.

title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists
summary: AI-Scientists arrived, but a world for them to grow in did not. Human scientists take theirs for granted $-$ centuries of open problems and shared ideas, waiting in the scientific literature. To AI-Scientists, that world is readable but not runnable, so we build Scientist World for them: every research paper becomes an executable environment. Our autonomous pipeline extracts each paper's open-ended research question and reproduces its proposed method as the baseline; an AI-Scientist entering the environment is evaluated against what the human authors achieved. We release the first 1,000 verified environments. With the world as an evaluation, we found that frontier AI-Scientists can already surpass the human researchers 74% of the time. As a record of how AI does science, it contains 6,400 hours of research traces, with every idea, experiment, failure, and success. As a training ground, we are able to raise (+158%) a small model to match frontier models in research ideation. At last, AI-Scientists' own world has arrived, grown from and growing with science itself.

AI.tldr: Introduces Scientist World, which turns research papers into executable environments, releases 1,000 verified ones, and finds frontier AI-Scientists surpass the human authors 74% of the time.
AI.motivation: Scientific literature is readable but not runnable for AI-Scientists, so they lack a world in which to pursue open problems and be evaluated against human research.
AI.method: An autonomous pipeline extracts each paper's open-ended research question and reproduces its proposed method as the baseline; an AI-Scientist entering the environment is evaluated against what the human authors achieved.
AI.result: The first 1,000 verified environments are released; frontier AI-Scientists surpass human researchers 74% of the time; the environments hold 6,400 hours of research traces; training raises a small model by +158% to match frontier models in research ideation.
AI.conclusion: The environments serve both as an evaluation of AI research ability and as a record and training ground for AI-driven science.

title: SteelAgent: LLM-Orchestrated, Physics-Informed Steel Property Prediction with Audited Generalization and Calibrated Uncertainty
comment: 10 pages, 3 tables. A shorter version of this work was published in the Proceedings of the Thirty-Fifth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-26), Demonstrations Track, pp. 8547-8550 (2026), doi:https://doi.org/10.24963/ijcai.2026/1000. Includes code for the synthetic experiment
summary: Steel property models can perform well on random test splits even when they extrapolate poorly to unfamiliar alloys. SteelAgent couples metallurgical descriptors and machine-learning models with a language-model interface for property prediction, uncertainty reporting and inverse design. We examine how the choice of held-out unit changes the conclusions drawn from SteelBench tensile-strength evaluations. For gradient boosting, pooled out-of-fold $R^2$ fell from 0.859 on a random split to 0.113 when steel families were held out. Empirical coverage of nominal 90% prediction intervals ranged from 91.0% under random splitting to 37.6% on held-out sources. The effect of physics-derived features depended on the evaluation. They increased gradient-boosting $R^2$ by 0.2534 in a 17-family holdout analysis and decreased it by 0.358 in a separate four-grade laboratory analysis. We report group-level errors and a synthetic regression experiment illustrating how calibration can deteriorate on held-out groups. These results motivate reporting the evaluation population alongside a property estimate or compliance score.

AI.tldr: Introduces SteelAgent, an LLM-orchestrated steel property predictor showing that random-split performance overstates generalization to unfamiliar steel families, with calibrated uncertainty reporting.
AI.motivation: Steel property models can perform well on random test splits yet extrapolate poorly to unfamiliar alloys, so conclusions depend on how held-out units are chosen.
AI.method: Couples metallurgical descriptors and machine-learning models with a language-model interface for property prediction, uncertainty reporting and inverse design, evaluated on SteelBench tensile-strength data with different held-out units.
AI.result: For gradient boosting, pooled out-of-fold R^2 fell from 0.859 on a random split to 0.113 when steel families were held out; empirical coverage of nominal 90% prediction intervals ranged from 91.0% under random splitting to 37.6% on held-out sources; physics-derived features raised gradient-boosting R^2 by 0.2534 in a 17-family holdout but lowered it by 0.358 in a four-grade laboratory analysis.
AI.conclusion: Property estimates and compliance scores should be reported together with the evaluation population, since calibration can deteriorate on held-out groups.

title: Certified folding-free deformable image registration: A whole-cell Jacobian certificate and a sequential variational solver
summary: Registration maps propagate labels, measure local volume change, and map results back through their inverses; requiring invertibility. Voxelwise checks can miss folds between grid points. We study the canonical continuous extension of a nodal displacement field by trilinear interpolation and give a test that proves its Jacobian determinant positive in every grid cell or rejects the map. The test is rigorous under IEEE 754 binary64 arithmetic (correct rounding, no contraction). With a fixed boundary, certification implies a bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism of the image domain. We introduce SeqVP, built around this certificate. A proximal Jacobian-determinant-curl formulation yields inner problems whose penalties on changes in the map, Jacobian determinant, and curl vanish to first order at the current iterate. The method decreases a fixed outer energy up to a floating-point resolution guard and certifies every committed iterate. After certified initialization, stopping at any time returns a folding-free map. A Poisson-preconditioned gradient method with Jacobian-aware step prediction and affine-scaling damping, initialized by certified handoff from an uncertified binary32 pre-optimizer, handles a 1 mm brain MRI with about 2e7 unknowns in 90 s on one GPU. On 49 held-out OASIS pairs, SeqVP achieves mean Dice 0.821 over 35 structures and 0.889 over 4 tissue classes, with certified zero folding. Gains are 0.022 and 0.025 over ANTs SyN, and 0.022 and 0.023 over uniGradICON with instance optimization at equal time (paired, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001), but maps are rougher. SeqVP is level with ANTs on LPBA40, behind it on IBSR18, and ahead of all label-free baselines on 20 large-deformation pairs. On fields from nine methods, the certificate finds non-positive-Jacobian cells in every ANTs SyN map (median 10, missed by voxelwise checks) and in maps from NiftyReg, ConvexAdam, uniGradICON, and TransMorph.

AI.tldr: Proves with a whole-cell Jacobian certificate that a trilinearly interpolated registration map is folding-free, and introduces SeqVP, a solver that keeps every committed iterate certified.
AI.motivation: Registration maps must be invertible to propagate labels and measure volume change, but voxelwise checks can miss folds between grid points.
AI.method: A test that certifies the Jacobian determinant is positive in every grid cell under IEEE 754 binary64 arithmetic; SeqVP combines a proximal Jacobian-determinant-curl formulation with certified initialization and handoff, and a Poisson-preconditioned gradient method with Jacobian-aware step prediction and affine-scaling damping.
AI.result: On 49 held-out OASIS pairs SeqVP reaches mean Dice 0.821 over 35 structures and 0.889 over 4 tissue classes with certified zero folding, 0.022 and 0.025 above ANTs SyN and 0.022 and 0.023 above uniGradICON with instance optimization at equal time (paired, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001), though its maps are rougher; a 1 mm brain MRI with about 2e7 unknowns is handled in 90 s on one GPU; the certificate finds non-positive-Jacobian cells in every ANTs SyN map (median 10, missed by voxelwise checks) and in maps from NiftyReg, ConvexAdam, uniGradICON and TransMorph.
AI.conclusion: Certification makes folding-free registration verifiable, and after certified initialization stopping SeqVP at any time returns a folding-free map.

title: Patch-Based Generalized Neural Texture Upscaling
summary: We propose a lightweight neural texture upscaling method. A single generalized MLP is trained on a diverse collection of texture patches and integrated into the texture sampling stage, upscaling low-resolution textures on-the-fly at rendering time. Because the model is generalized rather than overfit to specific content, no per-asset training is required - the same model applies to any existing scene without modifying texture data or the asset pipeline. Storing lower-resolution base textures reduces disk footprint, upscaling at sampling time eliminates the need to store high-resolution textures in VRAM, and sharing a single set of model weights across all textures ensures non-divergent GPU execution. We evaluate our method across multiple texture classes, demonstrating consistent improvement over analytic upscaling methods in perceptual quality.

AI.tldr: Proposes a single generalized MLP, trained on diverse texture patches, that upscales low-resolution textures on the fly during sampling, with no per-asset training.
AI.motivation: Storing high-resolution textures costs disk space and VRAM, and per-asset neural methods need training, so a general model that works on any existing scene is needed.
AI.method: A lightweight generalized MLP trained on a diverse collection of texture patches and integrated into the texture sampling stage, sharing one set of weights across all textures so GPU execution does not diverge.
AI.result: The abstract reports consistent perceptual improvement over analytic upscaling methods across multiple texture classes; it gives no numerical figures.
AI.conclusion: Storing low-resolution base textures with sampling-time neural upscaling can reduce disk and VRAM needs without modifying textures or the asset pipeline.

title: DC-SQEM: Medial Mesh Extraction by Dual Contouring with Spherical Quadric Error Metric
summary: The medial axis, as a compact representation, describes not only the boundary but also the interior of the shape, and has been widely used in analyzing and simplifying shapes. However, approximating feature-preserving medial axis from unstructured data, such as oriented point clouds, remains challenging due to the lack of explicit connectivity and the presence of noise in the source. We propose DC-SQEM, a dual-contouring-based framework that computes medial meshes (an explicit representation of the medial axis) directly from oriented point clouds without relying on watertight manifold surfaces or volumetric structures. With the help of an adaptive octree, our method fits local medial spheres for each cell based on the Spherical Quadric Error Metric (SQEM). We address several long-standing robustness issues in dual-contouring and mesh extraction, including out-of-cell solutions, unstable feature classification, and redundant topological connections. To this end, we introduce virtual nodes, a feature-downgrading strategy, and a geometry-driven topology-aware cleanup procedure, enabling robust SQEM-based medial dual contouring with clean mesh outputs. Unlike prior point-cloud-based methods that produce either only 1D skeletal structures or incomplete medial features, our method preserves sharp geometric features from the input and reconstructs a complete medial structure, including sheets, curves, seams, and junctions. Compared to restricted-power-diagram-based approaches, our algorithm can handle point clouds as input, without having a strong requirement on water-tightness or manifoldness.

AI.tldr: Proposes DC-SQEM, which extracts medial meshes directly from oriented point clouds by dual contouring with a Spherical Quadric Error Metric, reconstructing sheets, curves, seams and junctions.
AI.motivation: The medial axis is useful for shape analysis but hard to approximate from noisy unstructured point clouds, and prior point-cloud methods produce only 1D skeletons or incomplete medial features.
AI.method: An adaptive octree fits a local medial sphere per cell under the Spherical Quadric Error Metric; virtual nodes, a feature-downgrading strategy and a geometry-driven topology-aware cleanup address robustness issues in dual contouring.
AI.result: The method preserves sharp input features and reconstructs a complete medial structure, including sheets, curves, seams and junctions, without requiring watertight or manifold surfaces; the abstract reports no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: The approach produces clean medial meshes from point clouds, removing the watertightness and manifoldness requirements of restricted-power-diagram approaches.

title: Seeing Beyond the Next Step: World-Model-Guided Human-Like Navigation in Multi-Agent Scenes
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. 37 pages, 13 figures, 12 tables
summary: Selecting a next motion in a populated scene is not just a matter of avoiding what is currently in the way: an action can be locally feasible yet drift onto the road instead of the crosswalk, cut into a stream of crossing pedestrians, or bottleneck a narrow passage. These failure modes are invisible from the current state alone, and acting on them requires reasoning about what each candidate action will cause. World models offer exactly this, namely action-conditioned predictions of the future, but rolling them out at every decision step is a cost deployable navigation systems cannot pay, and the field has largely traded foresight for speed. We argue this is a false dichotomy. The natural place for a world model in human-aware navigation is at training time, as a preference oracle that distills foresight into a fast policy, rather than at inference time, as an online planner. We pair a discrete visual action prior with two task-aligned world models, one for nearby social dynamics and one for future scene semantics, that score candidate actions by their predicted consequences and refine the policy through group-relative preference distillation. At deployment, both world models are removed and the policy acts in a single forward pass. Across five held-out evaluation scenarios, this yields navigation that is simultaneously safer, more socially and group-coherent, and more goal-directed than strong reactive and learned baselines, with naive observers rating the resulting motion as more human-like. Taken together, our findings point to a different approach for bringing world-model foresight into deployable agents: not accelerating rollouts, but amortizing them into the policy so that the cost of looking ahead is confined to training. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: Proposes a navigation policy that uses world models only at training time as preference oracles to distil foresight, so that deployed navigation acts in a single forward pass.
AI.motivation: World models give action-conditioned foresight, but rolling them out at every decision step is too costly for deployable navigation systems, which have largely traded foresight for speed.
AI.method: A discrete visual action prior with two task-aligned world models, one for nearby social dynamics and one for future scene semantics, scores candidate actions by their predicted consequences and refines the policy through group-relative preference distillation; both world models are removed at deployment.
AI.result: Across five held-out evaluation scenarios the policy is safer, more socially and group-coherent and more goal-directed than strong reactive and learned baselines, and naive observers rate its motion as more human-like.
AI.conclusion: Amortizing world-model foresight into the policy confines the cost of looking ahead to training while keeping inference fast.

title: EDGAR: Efficient Diffusion-Driven Gaussian Avatar Refinement via Synthetic Failure
comment: Accepted to ACM Transactions on Graphics
summary: Recent advances in Gaussian splatting have enabled efficient and photorealistic head avatar reconstruction, yet monocular video-based or image-based methods still suffer from under-constrained geometry and texture, leading to artifacts such as blurring, stretching, and temporal instability. We present EDGAR (Efficient Diffusion-Driven Gaussian Avatar Refinement), a conditional diffusion framework designed to enhance the quality of Gaussian avatars by correcting artifacts while preserving identity fidelity. To train EDGAR, we construct EDGAR-SET, a hybrid triplet dataset composed of real-captured and synthetic-rendered samples, which simulates realistic Gaussian avatar failure cases by pairing degraded renderings with ground-truth and reference images. EDGAR refines degraded frames through a fusion block that injects identity features extracted by the self-supervised Sapiens model into a one-step diffusion backbone, enabling effective artifact removal without sacrificing efficiency. Our EDGAR model incorporates a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture to address diverse degradation types and severity levels. The refined multi-view renderings are subsequently used as pseudo-targets to optimize a single underlying Gaussian avatar, so that the final avatar can be rendered without applying EDGAR to every output frame. Experiments on three different Gaussian avatar reconstruction methods, each evaluated under three different settings, show improvements in both perceptual and reconstruction measures over the raw outputs and an SDEdit-style refinement baseline. In addition, cross-view evaluation demonstrates improved calibrated consistency, while tests under large yaw and open-mouth expressions verify robustness under extreme settings. These results collectively indicate a useful operating regime for recoverable appearance artifacts. The code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: Proposes EDGAR, a conditional one-step diffusion refiner with a Mixture-of-Experts that corrects artifacts in degraded Gaussian avatar renderings, whose refined views then supervise a single avatar.
AI.motivation: Monocular or image-based Gaussian avatars suffer from under-constrained geometry and texture, producing blurring, stretching and temporal instability.
AI.method: Trains on EDGAR-SET, a hybrid of real-captured and synthetic-rendered triplets that simulate avatar failures; a fusion block injects identity features from the Sapiens model into a one-step diffusion backbone; a Mixture-of-Experts handles diverse degradation types and severities; refined multi-view renderings serve as pseudo-targets to optimize one Gaussian avatar.
AI.result: Across three Gaussian avatar reconstruction methods under three settings, EDGAR improves perceptual and reconstruction measures over raw outputs and an SDEdit-style refinement baseline; cross-view evaluation shows improved calibrated consistency, and tests under large yaw and open-mouth expressions show robustness.
AI.conclusion: Refinement can serve as a training-time supervisor so the final avatar renders without applying diffusion to every frame, a useful regime for recoverable appearance artifacts.

title: Perception Over Geometry: Rethinking Gaussian Allocation in Mesh-based Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic novel-view synthesis but lacks explicit topology for geometric editing. Existing mesh-based methods enable geometric manipulation by associating Gaussians with triangular mesh faces, typically assigning a fixed number of Gaussians to each face. However, the representation capacity required for appearance reconstruction depends on local appearance complexity rather than merely on mesh tessellation density. To address these limitations, we propose P-MGS, a framework that separates appearance modeling from geometric control to achieve high quality rendering, compact representation, and flexible mesh editing. P-MGS introduces a perceptual complexity guided allocation strategy that distributes Gaussians according to surface appearance demand estimated from multiview observations. To preserve reconstruction flexibility, Gaussians are optimized without mesh constraints and subsequently associated with the original mesh through post hoc binding, retaining adaptive refinement while preserving mesh topology. During mesh editing, local affine deformation transfer updates Gaussian centers and covariances under mesh deformation, reducing misalignment and floating artifacts. Experiments demonstrate superior average novel view synthesis quality with fewer Gaussians and coherent mesh editing.

AI.tldr: Proposes P-MGS, which allocates Gaussians by perceived appearance complexity rather than mesh tessellation and binds them to the mesh after optimization, giving compact and editable mesh-based splatting.
AI.motivation: Mesh-based Gaussian splatting assigns a fixed number of Gaussians per triangular face, but the capacity needed for appearance depends on local appearance complexity rather than on tessellation density.
AI.method: Perceptual complexity guided allocation estimated from multiview observations; Gaussians are optimized without mesh constraints and then bound post hoc to the original mesh; local affine deformation transfer updates Gaussian centers and covariances during mesh editing.
AI.result: Average novel view synthesis quality is superior with fewer Gaussians, and mesh editing is coherent, with reduced misalignment and floating artifacts under deformation.
AI.conclusion: Separating appearance modelling from geometric control yields high-quality, compact and editable mesh-based Gaussian representations.

title: REACT: Towards Real-Time Completion of Skeletal Motion Signals
summary: Tracking user motion in interactive and immersive applications is increasingly common (e.g., video games, XR systems, smartphones). Yet, processing and transmitting human motion data remain critical challenges, as current approaches strongly rely on the quality of the tracked motion signals. In general, affordable motion-capture systems may produce unnatural animations in the presence of calibration errors, occlusions, sensor drift, high-frequency noise, or other artifacts. More specifically, we simulate occlusions and high-frequency noise and propose to mitigate their effects with REACT, an interactive online motion-completion framework operating causally, frame by frame, without look-ahead. REACT is an S4-based autoregressive model that coordinates complementary motion estimates under specific reliability-dependent constraints and exposes several interpretable internal signals. We present a system-level contribution consisting of a structured formulation of interactive motion completion together with a coherent instantiation of this formulation. We evaluate REACT against several causal baselines and architectural variants under varying levels of occlusion severity, and report their respective inference latencies. Our results show that REACT achieves a relevant compromise between reconstruction accuracy, update smoothness, and interactive inference. Finally, we characterize how its fusion behaviour changes under missing input observations.

AI.tldr: REACT is a causal, frame-by-frame online motion-completion framework built on an S4-based autoregressive model that repairs tracked skeletal motion corrupted by occlusions and high-frequency noise, balancing reconstruction accuracy, update smoothness and interactive inference latency.
AI.motivation: Motion tracking for games, XR and smartphones depends on signal quality, but affordable motion capture suffers from calibration errors, occlusions, sensor drift and noise, and processing and transmitting such data remains difficult.
AI.method: REACT coordinates complementary motion estimates under reliability-dependent constraints, exposes interpretable internal signals, and operates causally without look-ahead, with occlusion and high-frequency noise simulated for evaluation.
AI.result: REACT is compared with several causal baselines and architectural variants under varying occlusion severity, with inference latencies reported; it achieves a relevant compromise between reconstruction accuracy, update smoothness and interactive inference, and its fusion behaviour is characterised under missing input observations.
AI.conclusion: The paper gives a structured formulation of interactive motion completion together with a coherent instantiation, a system-level contribution toward robust real-time motion tracking.

title: T$^2$-Splat: Adaptive Topology Mesh Splatting with Texture Residuals
summary: Triangle-based splatting connects novel view synthesis with conventional graphics pipelines, but often requires excessive tessellation to preserve appearance details. We present T$^2$-Splat, which decouples topology adaptation from appearance refinement. Safe Restricted Delaunay Triangulation (Safe RDT) initializes mesh connectivity. Dynamic Topology Evolution (DTE) then adapts triangle allocation through edge collapse and vertex split operations. Residual per-face Mip-textures then refine appearance on the fixed mesh using scale-adaptive filtering. Experiments on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and DTU demonstrate competitive results with compact meshes. T$^2$-Splat improves PSNR by 0.71dB over MeshSplatting on Mip-NeRF 360. Additional compression experiments demonstrate flexible control of mesh complexity, supporting face budgets as low as 10% of the original face count. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: T2-Splat is a triangle-based splatting method that decouples adaptive mesh topology from appearance refinement, producing compact meshes for novel view synthesis; it improves PSNR by 0.71 dB over MeshSplatting on Mip-NeRF 360.
AI.motivation: Triangle-based splatting links novel view synthesis to conventional graphics pipelines, but it often requires excessive tessellation to preserve appearance details.
AI.method: Safe Restricted Delaunay Triangulation initializes mesh connectivity, Dynamic Topology Evolution adapts triangle allocation through edge collapse and vertex split, and residual per-face Mip-textures refine appearance on the fixed mesh using scale-adaptive filtering.
AI.result: Experiments on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks and Temples and DTU give competitive results with compact meshes; PSNR improves by 0.71 dB over MeshSplatting on Mip-NeRF 360; compression experiments support face budgets as low as 10% of the original face count.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling topology adaptation from appearance refinement yields compact meshes with flexible control of complexity while staying competitive in rendering quality.

title: Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. Project page: this https URL
summary: Knowledge of the hidden interior structure of an object, including the presence and location of cavities, is essential for predictive simulation, robotic manipulation, and nondestructive inspection. However, such cavities leave no direct signature on the static visible surface, making collision-induced deformation one of the few cues used to infer their presence. Structure from Collision (SfC) addresses this problem by recovering the hidden interior structure of an object from multiview observations of a collision event. SfC is challenging for two reasons: hidden cavities are only indirectly observable through surface motion, and voids correspond to the absence of material, making direct optimization using standard density representations difficult. The density-based SfC baseline inherits both difficulties. Surface-matching gradients do not directly indicate the cavity location, while density gradients can be weak or uninformative inside or near void regions. Therefore, we reformulate SfC as hypothesis-space reasoning, representing hidden cavities as explicit structural hypotheses whose variables encode available structural assumptions rather than relying on implicit density updates. A global stage performs gradient-free optimization over this hypothesis space using forward-only material point method (MPM) simulation. A local stage then refines the selected hypothesis as a Lagrangian particle system through gradient-based optimization using differentiable MPM simulation. On the SfC benchmark, our method improves hidden-structure reconstruction and future prediction over the density-based SfC baseline. Interior-topology stress tests and robustness analyses characterize its scope and limitations. The project page is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates Structure from Collision as hypothesis-space reasoning, recovering hidden cavities as explicit structural hypotheses through a gradient-free global search followed by gradient-based local refinement with differentiable MPM simulation, and improves hidden-structure reconstruction and future prediction over a density-based baseline.
AI.motivation: Cavities leave no direct signature on the visible surface, and density-based SfC is hard to optimize because surface-matching gradients do not indicate cavity location and density gradients are weak or uninformative near voids.
AI.method: Hidden cavities are represented as explicit structural hypotheses whose variables encode available structural assumptions; a global stage optimizes over this space without gradients using forward-only MPM simulation, and a local stage refines the selected hypothesis as a Lagrangian particle system with differentiable MPM.
AI.result: On the SfC benchmark the method improves hidden-structure reconstruction and future prediction over the density-based SfC baseline; interior-topology stress tests and robustness analyses characterize its scope and limitations.
AI.conclusion: Treating voids as explicit hypotheses rather than implicit density updates is a workable route to inferring interior structure from collision observations, with limits the paper delineates.

title: Hierarchical Incremental Beta Splatting for Online Reconstruction
comment: accepted to WACV 2027, project page: this https URL
summary: Online 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructs a scene during capture: each keyframe spawns primitives once and refines them for only a few dozen iterations, leaving little chance to fix poor initialization or missing detail. Gaussians are also inherently soft, needing many overlaps for solid surfaces. We present Hierarchical Incremental Beta Splatting (HIBS), which brings beta kernels to incremental reconstruction. Their shape parameter interpolates between a soft, Gaussian-like profile and a flat-topped, near-opaque surfel, acting as a confidence dial for geometry. Our confidence-aware spawning uses geometric observability and multi-view depth agreement to initialize both opacity and shape, producing solid primitives where geometry is verifiable and soft, correctable primitives where it is not. As online densification, error-driven relocation recycles stale primitives into photometric-error hotspots. Bounded beta kernel support enables exact tile culling and faster rasterization, and a closed-form, shape-preserving merging formulation provides a level-of-detail (LOD) hierarchy for fast optimization and real-time rendering. On Mip-NeRF 360 in the on-the-fly protocol, HIBS improves PSNR by up to 0.8 dB while reducing optimization time by up to 40%. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: HIBS brings beta kernels to online 3D Gaussian Splatting, using a shape parameter that interpolates between soft Gaussian-like and near-opaque surfel-like primitives; on Mip-NeRF 360 in the on-the-fly protocol it improves PSNR by up to 0.8 dB and cuts optimization time by up to 40%.
AI.motivation: Online 3DGS gets only a few dozen iterations per keyframe, leaving little chance to fix poor initialization or missing detail, and Gaussians are inherently soft, needing many overlaps to form solid surfaces.
AI.method: Confidence-aware spawning uses geometric observability and multi-view depth agreement to initialize opacity and shape, error-driven relocation recycles stale primitives into photometric-error hotspots, bounded beta kernel support enables exact tile culling, and a closed-form shape-preserving merge provides a level-of-detail hierarchy.
AI.result: On Mip-NeRF 360 in the on-the-fly protocol, HIBS improves PSNR by up to 0.8 dB while reducing optimization time by up to 40%.
AI.conclusion: Beta kernels with confidence-aware spawning and an LOD hierarchy make incremental reconstruction both more accurate and faster, supporting real-time rendering.

title: 4D Point Splatting for mmWave Radar Micro-Doppler Differentiable Rendering
summary: Millimeter-wave radar resolves the micrometer displacements of a moving body as micro-Doppler, enabling gait, gesture, activity, pose and vital-sign sensing. Each task relies on a downstream model trained on real data, yet radar datasets lag orders of magnitude behind vision and language. Brute-force collection will not close that gap, and existing synthesis methods (forward-only simulators, learned generators and static-scene inverse renderers) cannot fit a real capture of a moving body, leaving a sim2real gap. We present 4D Point Splatting (4DPS), a physics-based differentiable renderer that fits an explicit moving scene to a real capture. Using the synchronized camera to initialize the room and body, we represent the scene as oriented points carrying material, normal and velocity, and splat each point into range and Doppler bins. Our output is the raw complex return a real radar records, so we apply the same signal processing on the rendered data to obtain any representation for training any SOTA downstream model. We fit 235 sequences on HuPR and 100 on RT-Pose, two datasets with different radars. Our reconstructions set the state of the art, with median correlations of 0.940 and 0.830 on range-azimuth, 0.829 and 0.695 on range-Doppler, and 0.988 and 0.966 on micro-Doppler. Our renders also set the state of the art in downstream sim2real gap. On RT-Pose, a pose model trained on them reaches 21.9 cm MPJPE on real data, against 16.7 cm for real training and 127.6 cm for the RF-Genesis baseline, where both the rendered- and real-trained models learn nearly the same features. Our custom CUDA kernels fit a sequence in 5.7 minutes on HuPR and 12.9 on RT-Pose on one H100, making dataset-scale inverse rendering of mmWave radar possible for the first time. This work can enable synthetic data generation for any human-centered downstream task and model, and scene editing for data augmentation.

AI.tldr: 4D Point Splatting is a physics-based differentiable renderer that fits an explicit moving scene to a real capture and outputs raw mmWave radar returns for training downstream models, reporting state-of-the-art reconstructions and sim2real gap on HuPR and RT-Pose.
AI.motivation: Radar datasets lag orders of magnitude behind vision and language, and existing synthesis methods (forward-only simulators, learned generators, static-scene inverse renderers) cannot fit a real capture of a moving body, leaving a sim2real gap.
AI.method: Using the synchronized camera to initialize the room and body, the scene is represented as oriented points carrying material, normal and velocity, each splatted into range and Doppler bins; the output is the raw complex return a radar records, so the same signal processing can be applied, and custom CUDA kernels speed up fitting.
AI.result: Median correlations are 0.940 and 0.830 on range-azimuth, 0.829 and 0.695 on range-Doppler and 0.988 and 0.966 on micro-Doppler for HuPR and RT-Pose; on RT-Pose a pose model trained on renders reaches 21.9 cm MPJPE on real data, against 16.7 cm for real training and 127.6 cm for the RF-Genesis baseline; a sequence fits in 5.7 minutes on HuPR and 12.9 minutes on RT-Pose on one H100.
AI.conclusion: The renderer makes dataset-scale inverse rendering of mmWave radar feasible and can support synthetic data generation and scene editing for human-centered downstream tasks.

title: Uncertainty calibration in Bayesian M/EEG source imaging
summary: M/EEG source imaging requires accurate localization and reliable uncertainty estimates, yet posterior credible regions are rarely assessed for empirical calibration. We present a simulation-based framework for uncertainty quantification and calibration of empirical Bayesian inverse methods with closed-form conditional Gaussian posterior summaries. We compare Bayesian minimum norm (BMN) with sLORETA depth weighting and sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) with sparse basis field expansions (S-FLEX). S-FLEX allows retained coefficients to contribute nonzero marginal posterior variance at locations where voxel-wise SBL yields degenerate variances. For BMN, we derive joint source- and noise-variance updates through evidence maximization. We test whether adaptive noise learning yields near-calibrated uncertainties. Both methods retain residual miscalibration, motivating post-hoc isotonic recalibration of credible-region levels using empirical coverage. Simulations assess fixed- and free-orientation models across signal-to-noise ratios (SNR), source sparsity levels, and subject-specific head models, using oracle, baseline-estimated, and adaptively learned noise. Before recalibration, SBL+S-FLEX yields lower Wasserstein localization error, smaller posterior uncertainty, and coverage closer to nominal credibility than BMN+sLORETA. Isotonic recalibration improves both methods, with larger gains for conservative BMN+sLORETA posteriors; transfer across mismatched SNR, sparsity, and head models remains condition dependent. Noise specifications yield broadly consistent reconstruction and uncertainty trends within each estimator. In real auditory MEG data, SBL+S-FLEX provides more focal localization and tighter uncertainties than BMN+sLORETA, suggesting greater statistical power for identifying bilateral auditory sources.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a simulation-based framework to assess and recalibrate credible regions of empirical Bayesian M/EEG source imaging; before recalibration SBL with S-FLEX gives tighter, better-covered posteriors than BMN with sLORETA, and isotonic recalibration improves both methods.
AI.motivation: M/EEG source imaging needs accurate localization and reliable uncertainty estimates, yet posterior credible regions are rarely assessed for empirical calibration.
AI.method: Bayesian minimum norm (BMN) with sLORETA depth weighting is compared with sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) with sparse basis field expansions (S-FLEX) using closed-form conditional Gaussian posteriors; BMN gets joint source and noise variance updates via evidence maximization, and post-hoc isotonic recalibration adjusts credible-region levels using empirical coverage.
AI.result: Before recalibration SBL+S-FLEX gives lower Wasserstein localization error, smaller posterior uncertainty and coverage closer to nominal than BMN+sLORETA; isotonic recalibration improves both, with larger gains for BMN+sLORETA; transfer across mismatched SNR, sparsity and head models is condition dependent; in real auditory MEG data SBL+S-FLEX gives more focal localization and tighter uncertainties.
AI.conclusion: Both methods retain residual miscalibration, so recalibration is needed, and SBL+S-FLEX suggests greater statistical power for identifying bilateral auditory sources.

title: Big Models, Small Gains: Frozen Forecasters as Classifiers on MONSTER
comment: Asian Conference on Machine Learning, FMLTS Workshop, 2026
summary: Forecasting foundation models are increasingly used as frozen feature extractors for time series classification, but it remains unclear whether their pretrained representations offer an advantage over strong classifiers that do not require pretraining. This raises an important question: do these representations provide useful information beyond what the model architecture alone can capture, particularly when labelled data are scarce? We present a controlled benchmarking of two forecasting models, Reverso and Chronos-Bolt, on six large datasets from the MONSTER benchmark, using 1%, 10%, and 100% of the available training labels. We compare their frozen representations against four established time series classification methods and random-weight versions of the same forecasting models. Our results show that pretraining improves classification accuracy over random-weight counterparts on five of the six datasets, with gains of up to 23 percentage points. However, the frozen representations do not reliably outperform the strongest non-pretrained baseline in any setting: they perform worse in 15 of 17 settings and tie in the remaining two. Further experiments show that restoring amplitude information recovers part of the performance gap, while fine-tuning and forecast-error features do not close it. These findings highlight the importance of strong task specific baselines and random weight controls when evaluating forecasting foundation models for classification. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: On six MONSTER datasets with 1%, 10% and 100% of labels, frozen pretrained Reverso and Chronos-Bolt representations beat random-weight counterparts on five of six datasets but do not reliably outperform the strongest non-pretrained time series classifier.
AI.motivation: Forecasting foundation models are used as frozen feature extractors for time series classification, but it is unclear whether their pretrained representations help beyond strong classifiers that need no pretraining, especially when labels are scarce.
AI.method: Controlled benchmarking of Reverso and Chronos-Bolt against four established time series classification methods and random-weight versions of the same forecasting models, with further experiments restoring amplitude information and testing fine-tuning and forecast-error features.
AI.result: Pretraining improves accuracy over random weights on five of six datasets, with gains up to 23 percentage points; frozen representations perform worse than the strongest non-pretrained baseline in 15 of 17 settings and tie in the remaining two; restoring amplitude information recovers part of the gap, while fine-tuning and forecast-error features do not close it.
AI.conclusion: Strong task-specific baselines and random-weight controls are necessary when evaluating forecasting foundation models for classification.

title: Robust Stream Classification using Time Neutralising Decision Trees
comment: 33 pages, 9 Tables, 10 Figures. Accepted at Neurips 2026
summary: Data Streams are characterised as a potentially infinite source of data subject to non-stationarity. This non-stationarity, also called Concept Drift, often results in deployed predictive models having to be perpetually retrained as the underlying data generating process of the stream changes over time. Drift Detectors are a class of methods used to identify these changes, triggering these retraining procedures. Historically, Stream Learning has operated under the assumption that instances are only seen once, and cannot be stored for later use. Contemporary work relaxes this assumption, yet drift detection and simple resetting procedures are still ubiquitous. Building on related work which has shown that traditional Batch Learning algorithms often outperform Stream Learning algorithms when instances can be stored, we introduce Time Neutralising Trees (TNT), a Decision Tree architecture that enables robust stream classification in settings with Concept Drift. During training, TNT will filter out ("neutralise") old training samples that are no longer relevant given the current context of the stream. If those instances become relevant again, TNT will then re-include them. We evaluate TNT, and related algorithms on 24 real and semi-real classification data streams from the USP DS repository. Results show strong evidence that TNT achieves best-in-class performance on a wide-range of data streams with varying concept drift types.

AI.tldr: Time Neutralising Trees is a decision tree architecture for data streams with concept drift that filters out training samples no longer relevant to the current context and re-includes them when they become relevant again, reporting best-in-class performance across 24 real and semi-real streams from the USP DS repository.
AI.motivation: Stream learning still relies on drift detection and simple resetting, although stream learners relax the single-pass assumption and prior work shows batch learners often outperform stream learners when instances can be stored.
AI.method: TNT "neutralises" old training samples during training and re-includes them when they become relevant again, within a decision tree architecture.
AI.result: Evaluated on 24 real and semi-real classification streams from the USP DS repository against related algorithms, TNT shows, according to the abstract, strong evidence of best-in-class performance across a wide range of streams with varying concept drift types.
AI.conclusion: Relevance-based filtering of stored training instances offers a robust alternative to drift detection and resetting for stream classification under concept drift.

title: Stochastic Dynamics of Generative AI: From Autoregressive Models to Interacting LLM Networks and Neural SDEs
summary: This paper develops a stochastic dynamical-systems perspective on three classes of generative AI models. First, we formulate large language models (LLMs) as high-dimensional nonlinear autoregressive models with attention-based dependencies. This formulation connects pretraining by conditional maximum likelihood to sequential token generation and provides a probabilistic interpretation of LLM operation. Second, we consider networks of interacting LLMs and characterize their collective behavior through mean-field ordinary differential equations. These dynamics provide a framework for understanding emergent preferential attachment and persistent structural biases, including type-dependent glass-ceiling effects. Third, we consider neural stochastic differential equations (SDEs) as continuous-time generative models for stochastic trajectories, including those observed at irregular time intervals. We discuss their training with particular emphasis on Wiener-space cubature methods based on rough-path analysis as an efficient alternative to Monte Carlo estimation. Together, the three settings address probabilistic prediction, information exchange and emergent behavior in interacting networks, and path-space generative modeling.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a stochastic dynamical-systems view of three generative AI settings: LLMs as high-dimensional nonlinear autoregressive models, mean-field ODE dynamics of interacting LLM networks, and neural SDEs as continuous-time generative models.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to give one probabilistic and dynamical account of generative AI that connects pretraining, token generation, collective behaviour of interacting models and path-space generation.
AI.method: LLMs are formulated as nonlinear autoregressive models with attention-based dependencies, networks of interacting LLMs are analysed through mean-field ordinary differential equations, and neural SDEs are trained with Wiener-space cubature methods based on rough-path analysis as an alternative to Monte Carlo estimation.
AI.result: The abstract reports no numerical results; it states that the framework explains emergent preferential attachment and persistent structural biases, including type-dependent glass-ceiling effects, and discusses neural SDE training on trajectories observed at irregular time intervals.
AI.conclusion: The three settings together address probabilistic prediction, information exchange and emergent behaviour in interacting networks, and path-space generative modelling.

title: Finite-Time Convergence and Regret Guarantees for Neural Reinforcement Learning in POMDPs
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) in Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) is computationally challenging due to the curse of long-range dependence on history. Fortunately, recent studies have shown that a range of POMDPs that satisfy the filter stability assumption can be well approximated by a superstate Markov Decision Process (MDP) based on a truncated history in a finite-memory window, with a value gap that decays with the window length. However, existing finite-time convergence analyses on such superstate MDP surrogates are either limited to over-simplified linear function approximation or rely on an i.i.d. sampling oracle that is violated by POMDP trajectories, both of which severely limit the applicability of these theoretical results in practice. This motivates us to bridge the gap by investigating RL in POMDPs with nonlinear neural value function approximation. Our main contributions are threefold: i) We first establish a new finite-state MDP point-wise approximation error bound, which lays the foundation for our RL algorithm design and analysis in POMDPs; ii) By applying Temporal-Difference (TD) learning to POMDP-generated superstate transitions and targeting the Bellman fixed point of the superstate MDP, we prove a finite-time critic error bound with nonlinear neural value function approximation; and iii) By combining the neural critic function approximation error bound with the policy mirror descent framework, we obtain a finite-time sublinear regret against the optimal POMDP value. To the best of our knowledge, such a finite-time sublinear regret based on neural function approximation is the first in the literature for finite-memory POMDPs. Our numerical experiments also verify our theoretical results.

AI.tldr: For RL in POMDPs with neural value function approximation, the paper proves a finite-time critic error bound and a finite-time sublinear regret against the optimal POMDP value for finite-memory superstate MDP surrogates, and reports numerical experiments that verify the theory.
AI.motivation: Existing finite-time analyses of superstate MDP surrogates either are limited to linear function approximation or rely on an i.i.d. sampling oracle that POMDP trajectories violate, which limits their applicability.
AI.method: A new finite-state MDP point-wise approximation error bound is established; TD learning is applied to POMDP-generated superstate transitions to target the Bellman fixed point of the superstate MDP; the neural critic error is then combined with the policy mirror descent framework.
AI.result: The paper gives a finite-time critic error bound with nonlinear neural function approximation and a finite-time sublinear regret against the optimal POMDP value, which it claims is the first such neural result for finite-memory POMDPs; numerical experiments verify these results.
AI.conclusion: The analysis extends finite-time guarantees for superstate-based RL in POMDPs to nonlinear neural value functions without requiring an i.i.d. sampling oracle.

title: Shaping & Monitoring Models through their Internal Representations
summary: We propose Mechanistic Shaping, a unified framework for shaping models through their internal representations. Mechanistic Shaping is applied during training so that models follow specifications (rules) about which concepts they express, measured via their outputs or internal representations (e.g., no harmful content), and also which concepts they rely on, i.e., what they use to make their decisions (e.g., not a candidate's gender when screening a résumé). Across multiple domains (vision, medical imaging, language), scales (up to 32B parameters), and training paradigms (classification, SFT, DPO, GRPO), we find that Mechanistic Shaping substantially reduces targeted behaviors while preserving task performance. Since training against a representation can also modify it, we ask whether shaped concepts remain monitorable, a question that depends on the class of monitors considered. We therefore introduce a hierarchy of such classes, which separates a concept that escapes one probe from a concept that is truly gone. We characterize three geometric mechanisms of circumvention: the concept can drift away from the monitor, be erased from the layer, or persist in higher-order statistics as a nonlinear encoding, which we explain through a product-code construction. Although other mechanisms may arise in different settings or at larger scales, these three account for all of our observations, and each can be detected by a matching monitor. In practice, we find that shaped concepts largely remain monitorable: refitted linear probes recover the concept in most settings, and the original probe remains reliable whenever gradients do not flow through it. Taken together, these results point to the potential of using interpretability as a tool for training, and call for a correspondingly rigorous science of interpretability-based training.

AI.tldr: Mechanistic Shaping trains models against internal representations to reduce targeted concepts while preserving task performance across vision, medical imaging and language at up to 32B parameters, and the shaped concepts largely remain monitorable by refitted linear probes.
AI.motivation: Models should follow specifications about which concepts they express and rely on, but training against a representation can modify it, so it is unclear whether shaped concepts remain monitorable.
AI.method: Mechanistic Shaping is applied during training across classification, SFT, DPO and GRPO; a hierarchy of monitor classes separates a concept that escapes one probe from one truly gone; three geometric circumvention mechanisms are characterized: drift away from the monitor, erasure from the layer, and nonlinear encoding in higher-order statistics, explained by a product-code construction.
AI.result: Mechanistic Shaping substantially reduces targeted behaviours while preserving task performance; refitted linear probes recover the concept in most settings, and the original probe stays reliable whenever gradients do not flow through it.
AI.conclusion: The results point to interpretability as a training tool and call for a rigorous science of interpretability-based training, since the three mechanisms account for all observations so far.

title: Optimistic Hedge in General-Sum Games: Fundamental Limits and Regret Bounds via Temporal Approximation
summary: Optimistic Hedge, a multiplicative weight update with one step of extrapolation, is one of the most natural regret-minimizing dynamics for games, and characterizing its regret has been a longstanding open question. Daskalakis, Fishelson and Golowich proved that if all $m$ players in a finite general-sum game follow Optimistic Hedge with a fixed learning rate, each player's regret is polylogarithmic in the horizon $T$. Subsequently, Ha showed that an appropriate choice of learning rate makes each player's regret bounded independently of $T$. This bound, however, is non-constructive and its dependence on the number of actions $n$ is not explicit, leaving open whether Optimistic Hedge can achieve a constant regret bound which is polynomial in the size of the game. We show that the answer hinges on the number of players. In two-player games, there is a learning rate for which Optimistic Hedge guarantees $O(n\log n)$ regret independent of the horizon. In three-player games, however, no such bound is possible: for any learning rate up to an absolute constant and for sufficiently large horizon $T$, there is a game with $n$ actions per player in which some player's regret is $2^{\Omega(n)}$, and more generally, for every $m\ge3$ we construct $m$-player games in which some player's regret is $2^{\Omega(mn)}$; for learning rates above $2^{-\Omega(mn)}$, that player's regret even grows linearly in $T$. Our upper bound is based on a temporal approximation framework for the analysis of Optimistic Hedge. Starting from the variance-based RVU bound of Daskalakis et al., we approximate the losses over time-localized windows by well-behaved functions, whose total variation is a small fraction of their cumulative variance. In $m$-player games, the same framework gives a significantly simplified proof of the recent $O(\sqrt{m}\log n\log T)$ regret bound due to Ha.

AI.tldr: Optimistic Hedge has horizon-independent O(n log n) regret in two-player general-sum games for a suitable learning rate, but in games with three or more players some player's regret can be exponential in the number of actions; the upper bound uses a temporal approximation framework that also gives a simpler proof of Ha's O(sqrt(m) log n log T) bound.
AI.motivation: Whether Optimistic Hedge achieves constant regret polynomial in the game size was a longstanding open question, since Ha's bound is non-constructive and its dependence on the number of actions n is not explicit.
AI.method: Lower bounds come from explicit m-player games with n actions per player; the upper bound uses a temporal approximation framework that approximates losses over time-localized windows by well-behaved functions, starting from the RVU bound of Daskalakis, Fishelson and Golowich.
