AI.result: In two-player games a suitable learning rate gives O(n log n) regret independent of the horizon; in three-player games, for any learning rate up to an absolute constant and large enough T, some player's regret is 2^Omega(n); for every m at least 3 regret can be 2^Omega(mn), and for learning rates above 2^-Omega(mn) it grows linearly in T; the framework gives a much simpler proof of the O(sqrt(m) log n log T) regret bound.
AI.conclusion: The number of players decides whether Optimistic Hedge admits polynomial constant regret, and the temporal approximation framework simplifies the analysis of Optimistic Hedge.

title: Server-Side Sparse Assignment for Federated Mixture-of-Experts
comment: Accepted for publication in the proceedings of the 2026 IEEE Information Theory Workshop (ITW 2026)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly recognized for their remarkable capabilities; federated learning (FL) offers a promising framework for collaboratively fine-tuning LLMs on edge devices while achieving data privacy. However, edge devices are inherently heterogeneous: clients may exhibit diverse data distributions and resource constraints, including limited memory and computation budgets. Recent federated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches address these challenges by using sparse expert activation or partial expert loading. However, existing partial-expert methods rely on heuristic full-pool observations or prioritize system-wide load balance, without guarantees for recovering client-specific relevant experts from partial observations. We propose $S^3$-MoE, a server-side sparse expert assignment framework that estimates client-specific expert relevance from partial observations and refines assignments through an exploit--explore mechanism. We also establish relevance-estimation error and exact Top-$K$ recovery guarantees. Experiments using a CNN-based MoE on CIFAR-100 show that $S^3$-MoE recovers task-dependent client--expert preferences and reduces conflicts caused by correlated expert selection across clients. Compared with Full-20 FedAvg, which gives each client access to all 20 experts for local Top-5 routing, $S^3$-MoE achieves 1.31 percentage points higher mean final accuracy while loading only $5$ experts per client.

AI.tldr: S3-MoE is a server-side sparse expert assignment method for federated mixture-of-experts fine-tuning that estimates client-specific expert relevance from partial observations; on CIFAR-100 with a CNN-based MoE it reaches 1.31 percentage points higher mean final accuracy than Full-20 FedAvg while loading only 5 experts per client.
AI.motivation: Edge clients are heterogeneous in data and in memory and compute budgets, and existing partial-expert methods rely on heuristic full-pool observations or prioritize system-wide load balance, without guarantees for recovering client-relevant experts.
AI.method: The server estimates client-specific expert relevance from partial observations and refines assignments through an exploit-explore mechanism, with relevance-estimation error and exact Top-K recovery guarantees established.
AI.result: On CIFAR-100 with a CNN-based MoE, S3-MoE recovers task-dependent client-expert preferences and reduces conflicts caused by correlated expert selection; it achieves 1.31 percentage points higher mean final accuracy than Full-20 FedAvg, which gives each client all 20 experts for local Top-5 routing, while loading only 5 experts per client.
AI.conclusion: Server-side assignment from partial observations can reach higher accuracy with far fewer experts loaded per client, backed by theoretical recovery guarantees.

title: A Night at the LLM Zoo: Data Conditioned Flow Matching for Generating Pretrained LLM Weights
summary: A challenge to Weight Space Learning as it expands from task specific and vision models to Large Language Models (LLMs) is the absence of a well curated and analyzed LLM population. To address this, we train such a model zoo for application to Weight Space Generation by systematically varying the data mixture composition between web text, books, mathematics, coding, and French across populations of 51M, 124M, and 355M parameter GPT-2 Models, each tier with count N = 100. We analyze these populations by cosine similarity, functional diversity, Leave-One-Mixture-Out modeling, and variance decomposition. We show that the zoo contains diverse models whose variation is structured by training mixture composition. We embed the training mixture composition to condition a Flow Matching model of complete pretrained LLM weights in Gram-PCA compressed weight space. By demonstrating zero-shot generalization to held out mixtures, measuring Continuous Ranked Probability Score skill, as well as finding minimal changes in downstream test-set perplexity and general capability benchmark scores, we show that our generator generalizes on the simplex of data mixtures to produce models that perform similarly to those in the zoo ex nihilo. Finally, we produce all source code and artifacts to support the continued expansion of Weight Space Learning and Generation into the LLM domain.

AI.tldr: The authors train 100 GPT-2 models in each of three sizes (51M, 124M, 355M parameters) on varied data mixtures and use a data-conditioned Flow Matching model to generate complete pretrained weights for held-out mixtures, which perform similarly to zoo models on perplexity and benchmark scores.
AI.motivation: Weight Space Learning has lacked a well-curated and analysed LLM population, which is needed to extend it from task-specific and vision models to large language models.
AI.method: Models are trained with systematically varied mixtures of web text, books, mathematics, coding and French, and the population is analysed by cosine similarity, functional diversity, Leave-One-Mixture-Out modelling and variance decomposition; the mixture composition conditions a Flow Matching model of full weights in Gram-PCA compressed weight space.
AI.result: The generator shows zero-shot generalization to held-out mixtures, measured by Continuous Ranked Probability Score skill, with minimal changes in downstream test-set perplexity and general capability benchmark scores relative to zoo models.
AI.conclusion: The generator generalizes across the simplex of data mixtures to produce models that perform similarly to zoo models trained directly, and source code and artifacts are released to support weight space learning for LLMs.

title: Regulating Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand Operators with Fixed and Adaptive Penalties: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach
summary: Profit-maximizing Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand (AMoD) operators may exploit consumer surplus through excessive prices and underserve less profitable regions by relocating vehicles away from them. We study how penalty-based regulation of an AMoD operator in a multimodal mobility system can limit surge pricing and improve regional service availability. We model regulation as an outer control loop that acts on a learning-based operator. Static regulation with fixed penalties is formulated as a Markov Decision Process for an operator that jointly controls pricing and rebalancing, and dynamic regulation as a Partially Observable Stochastic Game in which a regulator periodically adjusts region-specific penalties in closed loop. Operator and regulator policies are learned with graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning. In experiments with real-world Manhattan data, fixed surge pricing penalties reduce the share of travelers facing excessive prices from 22% to 1%. For regional service availability, dynamic regulation improves the regulator's reward by up to 15.6% over fixed penalties of equal mean intensity. The gains in service availability are strongest when spare fleet capacity exists, whereas service deficits persist in peak periods with highly utilized fleets. The learned regulator policy responds by reducing penalties where limited fleet capacity restricts compliance. The results identify trade-offs between regulatory targets, operator profitability, and traveler utility.

AI.tldr: Using graph-based multi-agent RL on real Manhattan data, the paper shows that fixed surge-pricing penalties cut the share of travelers facing excessive prices from 22% to 1%, and dynamic regulation improves the regulator's reward by up to 15.6% over fixed penalties of equal mean intensity.
AI.motivation: Profit-maximizing Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand operators may exploit consumers through excessive prices and underserve less profitable regions by relocating vehicles away from them.
AI.method: Static regulation with fixed penalties is an MDP for an operator controlling pricing and rebalancing, and dynamic regulation is a partially observable stochastic game in which a regulator adjusts region-specific penalties in closed loop; both policies are learned with graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning.
AI.result: Fixed surge penalties reduce the share of travelers facing excessive prices from 22% to 1%; dynamic regulation improves the regulator's reward by up to 15.6% over equal-mean fixed penalties; service availability gains are strongest with spare fleet capacity, while deficits persist in peak periods with highly utilized fleets, and the learned regulator reduces penalties where limited capacity restricts compliance.
AI.conclusion: The results identify trade-offs among regulatory targets, operator profitability and traveler utility in multimodal mobility regulation.

title: Machine Learning for Live-Birth Prediction After IVF/ICSI From Structured Clinical Data: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Critical Appraisal
comment: 20 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables; supplementary material (26 pages) in ancillary files. Data and code: this https URL. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
summary: Machine-learning models predicting live birth after in vitro fertilisation (IVF) or intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) from routine clinical data report performance from near chance to near perfect. We systematically reviewed these models under PRISMA 2020, searching OpenAlex, Scopus and Web of Science to 22 October 2026, appraised them with PROBAST+AI and TRIPOD+AI, and pooled their discrimination with random-effects meta-analysis on the logit scale. We define what fixes the meaning of a model's output (decision point, endpoint, unit of analysis, data source) and map the 48 included studies by model family, decision point and validation design. Models evaluated only internally pooled to an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.814, against 0.756 (95% prediction interval 0.546-0.889) for models evaluated on a later period or another centre, and 0.764 for studies not at high risk of bias; neither difference was significant, and heterogeneity was extreme. Models whose decision point was not stated pooled to 0.910, the only significant moderator in meta-regression. Against logistic regression fitted to the same data, the best machine-learning model gained a pooled 0.056 AUC (95% CI 0.017-0.090). Of 48 studies, 47 were at high or unclear risk of bias, only four assessed the calibration slope, and no model has evidence of clinical impact. The certainty of the pooled evidence is low to very low; the gains that survive validation came from staging predictions to decision points and local calibration, not deeper architectures. We provide a TRIPOD+AI-mapped checklist, a benchmark specification and a research agenda.

AI.tldr: A PRISMA 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis of 48 studies finds that machine-learning models predicting IVF or ICSI live birth from structured clinical data pool to AUC 0.814 when evaluated only internally and 0.756 on later-period or other-centre validation, with extreme heterogeneity and low to very low certainty of evidence.
AI.motivation: Reported performance of machine-learning models for live birth after IVF or ICSI ranges from near chance to near perfect, so the validity and meaning of these models' outputs is unclear.
AI.method: The authors searched OpenAlex, Scopus and Web of Science under PRISMA 2020, appraised studies with PROBAST+AI and TRIPOD+AI, pooled discrimination with random-effects meta-analysis on the logit scale, and mapped studies by model family, decision point and validation design.
AI.result: Internally evaluated models pool to AUC 0.814, against 0.756 (95% prediction interval 0.546-0.889) for later-period or other-centre validation and 0.764 for studies not at high risk of bias, and neither difference is significant; models whose decision point was not stated pool to 0.910, the only significant meta-regression moderator; the best ML model gains a pooled 0.056 AUC (95% CI 0.017-0.090) over logistic regression on the same data; 47 of 48 studies are at high or unclear risk of bias, and only four assess calibration slope.
AI.conclusion: No model has evidence of clinical impact, and the authors supply a TRIPOD+AI-mapped checklist, a benchmark specification and a research agenda, arguing that the gains surviving validation came from staging predictions to decision points and local calibration rather than deeper architectures.

title: Data-Driven Modeling of Molten Chloride Corrosion Using Static Test Data
summary: Molten chloride corrosion has been studied for decades, yet reliable prediction across different alloys, salts, and test conditions remains difficult. In this work, 291 static molten chloride corrosion experiments reported in the literature were compiled into a structured dataset and used to develop an interpretable machine-learning framework for corrosion-rate predictions. To better represent the differences in salt condition across studies, a Chloride Salt Preparation Index (CSPI) was introduced to bring the reported salt-treatment method, atmosphere control, and pre-exposure impurity condition on a common numerical scale. A blended tree-based ensemble provided the most consistent predictive performance, achieving a cross-validated \(R^2\) of 0.85 and an MAE of 0.41 mg cm\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\). The graded CSPI retained more useful information than a simple purified/unpurified classification and emerged as the dominant model descriptor. Global sensitivity and SHAP analyses further identified exposure time, temperature, and alloy chemistry as important contributors to the model predictions, with several observed trends consistent with the established molten-chloride corrosion behavior. The conformal prediction intervals were well calibrated, providing an estimate of prediction uncertainty in addition to the point prediction. Overall, the framework demonstrates that historical corrosion data can support quantitative, interpretable, and uncertainty-aware prediction when experimental context is represented explicitly, while also highlighting where more consistent reporting and targeted experiments are needed to improve future molten-salt corrosion models.

AI.tldr: A blended tree-based ensemble trained on 291 literature static molten chloride corrosion experiments predicts corrosion rate with cross-validated R2 of 0.85 and MAE of 0.41 mg cm-2 day-1, with a graded Chloride Salt Preparation Index emerging as the dominant descriptor.
AI.motivation: Reliable prediction of molten chloride corrosion across alloys, salts and test conditions remains difficult, and salt-preparation conditions differ between studies in ways that are hard to compare.
AI.method: The 291 experiments are compiled into a structured dataset; a Chloride Salt Preparation Index encodes salt treatment, atmosphere control and pre-exposure impurity condition on one numerical scale; a blended tree-based ensemble is used with global sensitivity analysis, SHAP analysis and conformal prediction intervals.
AI.result: The ensemble achieves cross-validated R2 of 0.85 and MAE of 0.41 mg cm-2 day-1; the graded index retained more useful information than a simple purified/unpurified classification and is the dominant descriptor; exposure time, temperature and alloy chemistry are also important contributors, and the conformal prediction intervals are well calibrated.
AI.conclusion: Historical corrosion data can support quantitative, interpretable and uncertainty-aware prediction when experimental context is represented explicitly, and the work highlights where more consistent reporting and targeted experiments are needed.

title: Scalable Bayesian Gaussian Process Classification for Cancer Histopathology: Calibrated Uncertainty Under Distribution Shift
summary: Reliable uncertainty quantification is essential for clinical deployment of cancer diagnosis models, yet neural networks and variational Gaussian process methods can produce overconfident predictions, particularly under the distribution shifts that arise when models trained at one hospital are applied at another. We present a scalable Bayesian Gaussian Process Classification (GPC) framework that operates on frozen pathology foundation model embeddings (Phikon) and combines accelerated Randomly Pivoted Cholesky (RPCholesky) for low-rank kernel factorization, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) with non-centered parameterization for posterior sampling, and a pivots-as-inducing-points scheme for prediction. This makes HMC posterior sampling in the low-rank latent representation tractable at N approximately 300,000 training points, enabling HC-based low-rank GPC on substantially larger datasets than prior MCMC-based demonstrations. We evaluate on two histopathology benchmarks for breast cancer metastasis detection: PCam and CAMELYON17-WILDS, where the latter tests calibration under hospital-level distribution shift. Compared to stochastic variational GP and neural network baselines, our method improves calibration and predictive performance - reducing expected calibration error by up to 88% and false negative rate by up to 90% - with the largest gains appearing under distribution shift, suggesting that HMC-based posterior sampling provides more trustworthy uncertainty estimates for cross-site pathology classification.

AI.tldr: A scalable Bayesian Gaussian process classifier on frozen Phikon pathology embeddings, using accelerated randomly pivoted Cholesky factorization and HMC, reduces expected calibration error by up to 88% and false negative rate by up to 90% relative to stochastic variational GP and neural baselines for breast cancer metastasis detection, with the largest gains under hospital-level shift.
AI.motivation: Neural networks and variational GP methods can be overconfident, particularly when a model trained at one hospital is applied at another, which is a problem for clinical deployment.
AI.method: Accelerated RPCholesky low-rank kernel factorization, HMC with non-centered parameterization for posterior sampling in the low-rank latent representation at about 300,000 training points, and a pivots-as-inducing-points scheme for prediction.
AI.result: On PCam and CAMELYON17-WILDS, compared with stochastic variational GP and neural network baselines, the method improves calibration and predictive performance, reducing expected calibration error by up to 88% and false negative rate by up to 90%, with the largest gains under distribution shift.
AI.conclusion: HMC-based posterior sampling gives more trustworthy uncertainty estimates for cross-site pathology classification, and the method makes HMC-based low-rank GPC feasible on much larger datasets than prior MCMC demonstrations.

title: Teaching Agents the "Principle", Not the "Reward"
summary: Reinforcement learning has achieved strong performance in many tasks by letting agents learn from nothing more than a reward signal. However, in more complex tasks, agents still struggle to learn good, generalizable policies, even with carefully designed rewards and abundant samples. We argue that this difficulty stems from the reward decoding burden: designers encode their knowledge of the desired behavior into rewards and penalties, and agents must infer this knowledge from long sequences of noisy scalars. To address this burden, we propose prescriptive policy learning (PPL), which directly teaches agents higher-level knowledge about the tasks, termed principles of behavior, such as how to maintain balance, how to accumulate energy, and how to land smoothly. Through appropriately selected key quantities and references, PPL can directly indicate at every step whether the agent follows the principles and to what extent. Our experiments show that agents can learn good, generalizable policies without any reward. Taught only simple heuristic principles, PPL agents outperform reward-based methods with far fewer samples. Their policies also transfer directly to harder settings and keep performing well, demonstrating their strong generalization ability. In summary, PPL provides a new approach in which rough knowledge of the desired behavior is enough for agents to learn good, generalizable policies, even when the system dynamics cannot be accurately modeled.

AI.tldr: Prescriptive policy learning teaches RL agents high-level principles of behaviour, such as maintaining balance or landing smoothly, instead of relying on reward signals; agents taught only simple heuristic principles outperform reward-based methods with far fewer samples and transfer to harder settings.
AI.motivation: Agents struggle to learn good, generalizable policies in complex tasks even with carefully designed rewards, because they must infer the designer's knowledge from long sequences of noisy scalar rewards.
AI.method: Prescriptive policy learning (PPL) uses appropriately selected key quantities and references to indicate at every step whether the agent follows the principles of behaviour and to what extent.
AI.result: Agents learn good, generalizable policies without any reward; PPL agents outperform reward-based methods with far fewer samples, and their policies transfer directly to harder settings and keep performing well.
AI.conclusion: Rough knowledge of the desired behaviour is enough for agents to learn good, generalizable policies, even when system dynamics cannot be accurately modelled.

title: Depth or Description? When a One-Step Latent Score Replaces Lookahead in Proactive Information Acquisition
summary: A proactive agent must decide what to ask before it acts. Exact lookahead values combinations of questions but is expensive and leans on a fitted model; a one-step score is cheap but can miss them. Our main finding: the need for depth often lies in how the hidden cause is described. A one-step score on the label can be blind to an interaction among answers. A score on a suitable latent cause is not, and where that latent encodes the decision it replaces most of depth at a fraction of the search.
